Repraesentiva illa Romana adversatur Christi verbo, ac proinde ab illius sententiâ nullus fidelium dependere debet vel potest; A quibus autem sincerè propagetur veritas christiana, judicetur secundum scripturas S. Equidem, quicunque habent oculos à spiritu Dei illuminatos, facilè agnoscent in ecclesiis nostris sonare integram legis, & euangelii doctrinam,
units.tr: 49[?]. In so great a variety of teachers, no one can be certain where the saving truth and the orthodox faith are, if it were lawful with impunity to depart from that so-called representative Roman church, which has flourished for so many centuries. Answer: That representative Roman church is opposed to the word of Christ, and therefore no believer ought or is able to depend upon its judgment. But by whom the Christian truth is sincerely propagated is to be judged according to the Holy Scriptures. Indeed, whoever have eyes illumined by the Spirit of God will readily recognise that in our churches the whole doctrine of the law and the gospel resounds,

units.la: DE JURE PROTESTAN-TIUM ORTHODOXORUM CONTRA concilium Tridentinum, & reliquas pontificiorum Romanorū syn-odos & conventus ; eo-rūmq; constitutiones atq; anathe-mata.
units.tr: On the Right of the Orthodox Protestants Against the Council of Trent and the Other Synods and Assemblies of the Roman Pontiffs, and Their Constitutions and Anathemas.

units.la: QUÆRITUR an jure protestan-tes rejiciant auctoritatem concilii Tridentini caeterarumq; synodorum, quae sunt ad praescriptum & sententiam pontificum Romanorū indicta? Rō. pontificii negant. Orthodoxi pro-testantes affirmant.
units.tr: The question is whether Protestants rightly reject the authority of the Council of Trent and of the other synods that have been summoned according to the prescription and judgment of the Roman pontiffs. The Roman Papists deny it. The orthodox Protestants affirm it.

units.la: Affirmativam sequentibus rationibus probamus. Nam ex historia sacra cō-stat, omnes solennes conventus & synodos in populo Dei esse convo-catas non à sacerdotibus; sed à gu-bernatoribus populi (qui videlicet fuerunt professione ecclesiae membra) horum item auctoritate cultus impios atque idololatricos esse sublatos, latos, & contrà verum Dei cultum restitutum ac stabilitum.
units.tr: We prove the affirmative by the following arguments. For it is clear from sacred history that all the solemn assemblies and synods among the people of God were convoked not by priests but by the rulers of the people (who, of course, were members of the Church by profession). By their authority also the impious and idolatrous worship was abolished and, on the contrary, the true worship of God was restored and established.

units.la: Ita Deut. 29 Moses dicitur convocasse omnes Israelitas ex Domini mandato, ut pangeret cum filiis Israelis. Similiter Ios. 23. legitur Iosua, tanquam princeps populi convocasse totum Israelem, seniores ejus & primores. Item cap. 24. dicitur congregasse omnes tribus Israelis, postquam convocasset seniores Israelis & primores ejus, hoc fine, ut eos ad perseverantiam in vero Dei cultu exhortaretur, ac fœdus inter Deum & Israelitas renovaret. 2. Sam. 6. idem legitur de rege Davide, quòd congregarit quosq; delectos ex Israele ad restaurandum Dei cultum. Idem scribitur Reg. 8. de Solomone, quòd jusserit congregari seniores Israelis, & omnes primarios tribuum, postea quam instituere decrevisset certa cultus divini formam, ex præscripto Dei. 2. Chron. 29. Ezechias confirmavit sacerdotes; item jussit convenire sacerdotes & Levitas, ad restaurandum verum Dei cultum. et cap 30. Legitur, iniuisse consilium & regem & principes ejus cum tota congregatione, de celebrando paschate, mense secundo. 2. Chron. 34. & 35. Josia similiter dicitur cōgregasse omnes seniores Judæ & Hierosolimorū, & constituisse sacerdotes in custodiis suis, & confirmasse eos in ministerio domus DOMINI.
units.tr: Thus in Deut. 29 Moses is said to have summoned all the Israelites by the Lord's command, that he might make a covenant with the children of Israel. Similarly, Josh. 23 reads that Joshua, as prince of the people, summoned all Israel, its elders and its leaders. Likewise, chap. 24 says he gathered all the tribes of Israel, after he had summoned the elders and leaders of Israel, with this aim: that he might exhort them to persevere in the true worship of God and renew the covenant between God and the Israelites. 2 Sam. 6 reads the same of King David, that he gathered chosen men from Israel to restore the worship of God. The same is written in Kings 8 of Solomon, that he ordered the elders of Israel and all the chief men of the tribes to be gathered, after he had decided to establish a certain form of divine worship according to the prescription of God. 2 Chron. 29: Hezekiah consecrated the priests; he also ordered the priests and Levites to assemble to restore the true worship of God. And chap. 30 reads that the king and his princes with the whole congregation took counsel about celebrating the Passover in the second month. 2 Chron. 34 and 35: Josiah likewise is said to have gathered all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem, and to have set the priests in their charges and confirmed them in the ministry of the house of the LORD.

units.la: Deinde Psal. 119. docetur, quòd verbum Domini sit lucerna pedibus nostris. & Jerem. 8. v. 9. Ecce, inquit, verbum Domini spernunt, & cuius rei sapientia inesser[?] eis?
units.tr: Then Psalm 119 teaches that the word of the Lord is a lamp to our feet. And Jer. 8:9: "Behold," he says, "they reject the word of the Lord; what wisdom is in them?"

units.la: Similiter vult Christus Joh. 5, ut omnes scrutetur scripturas. & Paulus Gal. 1. 8. 9. ita tenaciter omnes & singulos verbo Dei ( in scripturis consignato) adhærere vult, ut pronunciet anathema esse, si quis, vel etiam angelus è cœlo, euangelizaret præter id quod accepimus. Item. 2. Tim. 3. 16. dicitur omnis scriptura diuinitus inspirata utilis esse ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam in iustitia, ut perfectus sit homo Dei ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructus. & 2. Pet. 1. 19 docetur, quòd habemus firmissimum sermonem illū propheticum: quodque bene faciunt quicunque attendunt, velut lucernam splendentem in obscuro loco, usque dum dies illucescat, & lucifer oriatur in cordibus nostris.
units.tr: Likewise Christ wills in John 5 that all should search the Scriptures. And Paul in Gal. 1:8, 9 wills that all and each adhere so tenaciously to the word of God (set down in the Scriptures) that he pronounces anathema on anyone who, even an angel from heaven, should preach to us beside what we have received. Also in 2 Tim. 3:16 it is said that all Scripture, divinely inspired, is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for discipline in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work. And in 2 Pet. 1:19 it is taught that we have the most sure prophetic word, and that they do well who heed it, as a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts.

units.la: Præterea Psal. 1. 1. dicitur beatus esse vir ille, qui non ambulat in consilio impiorum, & viæ improborum non insistit, & in consessu derisorum non desidet.
units.tr: Moreover, Psalm 1:1 says that blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers.

units.la: Denique act. 15. 6. & 22. legitur, quòd omnes apostoli, etiam Petrus ipse, adfuerint personaliter, quodque posteaquam magna conquisitio facta esset, communi tam laicorum quàm clericorum consilio in synodo apostolica controversia sit tractata & definita. nam his verbis concipitur decretum: Tunc visum est apostolis & presbyteris cum totâ ecclesia. Ex his manifestū est, quę & quali a s. scriptura exigat concilia & synodos: videlicet; In quibus totus populus, vel omnes ecclesiæ, quantum fieri potest, comprimis vero illæ, quarum interest, conveniant, vel saltem viri primarii ex omni statu ecclesiæ, nullo item excluso, qui audire requirat ea quæ sunt tractanda, quæq; ad doctrinam & mores pertinent.
units.tr: Finally, Acts 15:6 and 22 reads that all the apostles, Peter himself included, were present in person, and that after much debate had taken place, the controversy was discussed and settled in the apostolic synod by the common counsel of laity and clergy alike. For the decree is framed in these words: "It seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole Church." From this it is plain what kind of assemblies and synods Scripture requires, and how they should be constituted: namely, those in which the whole people, or all the churches, as far as possible, assemble; or at least those whom it concerns, and especially the leading men from every rank of the Church, no one being excluded, who wish to hear the matters to be dealt with, which pertain to doctrine and morals.

units.la: 2. Deinde quòd jus convocandi concilii, præsertim universale, præcipuè spectet ad magistratum politicum, si Christianus sit.
units.tr: 2. Next, the right to convoke a council, especially a universal one, belongs chiefly to the civil magistrate, if he is a Christian.

units.la: 3. Præterea quòd de controversiis ac querelis, non ex humanis traditionibus & pontificum decretis, neque etiam ex pluralitate suffragiorū; sed juxta solius verbi Dei normam sit judicandum: neque ulli liceat etiam angelo, nedum homini, vel tantillum verbo Dei detrahere aut adjicere.
units.tr: 3. Moreover, controversies and disputes are to be judged not by human traditions and the decrees of the pontiffs, nor by a plurality of votes, but solely according to the rule of God's Word; and it is not lawful for anyone, not even an angel, much less a man, to take away from or add to the Word of God in the least.

units.la: 4. Ad hæc quòd rejiciendi sint, quantum fieri potest, homines improbi, sycophantæ, ad sophisticen & flexiloquas conciliationes assuefacti; & contrà colligendi in qualibet provincià ii, quos constat doctrinâ & vitæ integritate excellere, quique non solo nomine & titulo gaudent, sed reipsa episcopi sunt; hoc est ecclesiarum & ministerii inspectores, theologi, doctores &c. qui etiam sunt pacis & veritatis studiosi, aperti, candidi.
units.tr: 4. Furthermore, wicked men, sycophants, and those accustomed to sophistry and to smooth-tongued compromises are to be rejected as far as possible; and, on the contrary, those are to be gathered in every province who are known to excel in doctrine and integrity of life, who rejoice not only in the name and title but are in fact bishops, that is, overseers of the churches and of the ministry: theologians, teachers, and so on, who are also lovers of peace and truth, open and sincere.

units.la: 5. Porrò quòd concilia non sint alligata certorum hominum auctoritati, sed curandum, ut Spiritus s. in nullo prorsus negligatur; ac proinde cuivis etiam infimo detur dicendi locus, & quidem ab utraque parte: ita tamen ut omnia legitimè atque ordine fiant.
units.tr: 5. Again, councils are not to be bound to the authority of certain men, but care must be taken that the Holy Spirit is in no way neglected; and accordingly every person, even the lowliest, is to be given a place to speak, and indeed from either side, provided that everything is done lawfully and in good order.

units.la: 6. Denique quòd hic sit verus finis synodorum, ut iis idololatria atque errores, comprimis qui evertunt fundamentum, tollantur; & contrà pura doctrina & verus Dei cultus sanctè asserantur, vulnera ecclesiæ sanentur, discordiæ omnes collantur, pax & concordia confti-tuatur & conservetur.
units.tr: 6. Finally, the true purpose of synods is this: that idolatry and errors, especially those that overthrow the foundation, be removed; and on the contrary, that pure doctrine and the true worship of God be solemnly affirmed, the wounds of the Church be healed, all dissensions be composed, and peace and concord be established and preserved.

units.la: At contrà in concilio Tridenti-no & reliquis pontificiorum synodis convenerunt tātum jurati pontificis Romani Cardinales, episcopi, prælati: arctisimo vinculo pontifici obstricti.
units.tr: But, on the contrary, at the Council of Trent and the other synods of the Papists there assembled only the cardinals, bishops, and prelates of the Roman pontiff, sworn to him and bound to him by the tightest bond.

units.la: 2. Indictio concilii facta est non ab imperatore, vel alio rege vel principe politico; sed à pontifice Romano.
units.tr: 2. The council was summoned not by the emperor, or another king or civil prince, but by the Roman pontiff.

units.la: 3. De controversiis non licuit illic judicari ex solis scripturis sacris propheticis & apostolicis proprie dictis; sed juxta suffragiorum episcopalium pluralitatem, & juxta traditiones ecclesiæ Romanæ, neque quicquam fuit ratum, ante pontificis confirmationem.
units.tr: 3. Controversies could not there be judged from the sacred prophetic and apostolic Scriptures alone, properly so called, but according to the plurality of episcopal votes and according to the traditions of the Roman Church; nor was anything ratified before the pontiff's confirmation.

units.la: 4. Nulli sunt admissi, nisi qui se-se subjecisent pontificis auctori-ta-ti & decretis; neque quicquam auditum fuit de relaxatione juramenti, quo pontifex sibi clerū suū obstrin-xisse legitur. de quo vide plura apud Ja-
units.tr: 4. No one was admitted except those who had submitted themselves to the pontiff's authority and decrees; nor was anything heard of a release from the oath by which the pontiff is read to have bound his clergy to himself. On which see more in Ja-

units.la: 5. Soli episcopi Romani fuerunt judices & vocem decisivam habuerunt; vel potius solus papa cum suis mancipiis summam præsidendi, judicandi, & decidendi auctoritatem sibi arrogavit: ab eoque munere omnes aliorum ordinum viros, atque etiā ipsos reges & principes omnino exclusit.
units.tr: 5. The Roman bishop alone was judge and had the decisive vote; or rather, the pope alone, with his creatures, arrogated to himself the supreme authority of presiding, judging, and deciding, and totally excluded from that office men of all other orders, and even kings and princes themselves.

units.la: 6. Finem denique hunc sibi revera propositum habuerunt, ut continuarent & confirmarent omnia illa decreta, quæ antea partim falsa, partim ambigua in synodis pontificiis fuerant edita, utque omnibus modis tuerentur idololatriam & sedem pontificis Romani; ut deinceps quoque ex plenitudine potestatis mandaret quicquid vellet: ac proinde nihil profuit ad tollendum, quæ irrepserant in ecclesiam, corruptelas & morbos alios: sed contra occasionem & materiam præbuit majoribus discordiis persecutionibus, bellis, & lanienis. Merito itaque concludimus, in Tridentino illo genuinam Christiani & legitimi concilii formam videri non posse.
units.tr: 6. Finally, they really had this as their aim: to continue and confirm all those decrees which had previously been issued in the papal synods, partly false and partly ambiguous, and to defend in every way the idolatry and the see of the Roman pontiff, so that henceforth too he might command whatever he wished from the fullness of his power. Accordingly, it did nothing to remove the corruptions and other diseases that had crept into the Church; but on the contrary it provided the occasion and material for greater dissensions, persecutions, wars, and slaughters. Rightly, therefore, we conclude that the form of a genuine Christian and lawful council cannot be seen in that Tridentine assembly.

units.la: His adde rationes sequentes: 1. Quod convocatio merito institui debet ab eo, qui habet superioritatem, ut loquuntur, & jurisdictionem aliquam in eos quos vocat; at Romano pontifici nulla competit in ecclesias totius Orientis & Occidentis jurisdictio aut superioritas, neq; in spiritualibus neq; corporalibus: sicut prolixius demonstratur in loco de pontifice Romano.
units.tr: To these add the following arguments: 1. Because a convocation ought rightly to be instituted by one who has superiority, as they say, and some jurisdiction over those whom he summons; but no jurisdiction or superiority belongs to the Roman pontiff over the churches of the whole East and West, either in spiritual or in temporal matters, as is shown at greater length in the place on the Roman pontiff.

units.la: 2. Deinde neutiquam tunc temporis jus convocandi concilium concedi potuit vel debuit pontifici: quia ipse cum suis cardinalib. & reliquis juratis fuit reus & pars litigantium. Nullo autem jure, qui vel reus vel actor est, potest sibi sumere superioritatem & jus convocandi, aut judicis vel superioris personam eodem judicio sustinere.
units.tr: 2. Furthermore, at that time the right to convene a council could by no means have been granted to the pope, or ought to have been. He himself, with his cardinals and the rest of his sworn men, was a defendant and a party to the dispute. But by no law can one who is either defendant or plaintiff claim for himself superiority and the right to convene, or take on the role of judge or superior in the same trial.

units.la: 3. Neq; illud Tridentinum fuit instiinstitutum loco tuto, & tali, qui con-veniret concilio pio & libero: sed, contrà elegerunt locum talem, qui fuit aditu difficillimus & periculo-sissimus parti adversæ pontificis im-pietatem accusaturæ: At indubitati juris est, quòd tum personæ tum ipsi causæ, de quâ agendum sit, locus ju-dicii tutus esse debeat, neq; ullus in loco suspecto comparere teneatur, idq; potissimum propter sententias dicendas, quas imprimis liberas esse oportet.
units.tr: 3. Nor was that Council of Trent established in a safe place, or one suited to a pious and free council. On the contrary, they chose a place that was very difficult to reach and very dangerous for the opposing party, which was going to accuse the pope of impiety. But it is a matter of indisputable law that both the persons and the very case to be argued must have a safe place of trial, and that no one is bound to appear in a suspect place, chiefly because of the opinions to be delivered, which above all ought to be free.

units.la: 4. Quibus adde, quod in plurib. Imperii comitiis publicis sit decre-tum, concilium liberum atq; Christianum in ipsa Germania, loco op-portuno, instituì debere: Tridentū vero nō Germaniæ sed Italiæ oppi-dum est, multo minus libera imperii civitas est, sed tali episcopo par et, qui etiam ipse ad exemplum reliquorum ecclesiasticorum fide & jurejurando pontifici Romano est obstrictus: quocirca etiam omnia pontificia excommunicationis fulmina, omnesq; censuræ, aggravatio-nes, excommunicationes editæ per bullam cœnæ, & cætera pontificum præjudicia, in toto illo episcopatu auctoritatem suam integram habet: nec minùs illud injustum Constan-tiensis synodi concilium de fide hæ-reticis non servandâ.
units.tr: 4. To these add that, in several public diets of the Empire, it was decreed that a free and Christian council should be held in Germany itself, in a suitable place. Trent, however, is a town not in Germany but in Italy, and far from being a free imperial city, it belongs to a bishop who, like the other ecclesiastics, is bound to the Roman pope by oath and fealty. For this reason, all the papal thunderbolts of excommunication, all the censures, aggravations and excommunications issued through the Bull of the Lord's Supper, and the other prejudgments of the popes, keep their full authority throughout that whole bishopric. Nor is the unjust decision of the Council of Constance, that faith need not be kept with heretics, any less in force.

units.la: 5. Nihil equidem gravius aut difficilius piis principibus tunc temporis accidere potuit, in tanta perturbatione rerum omnium, quàm quòd adeò procul & in longinquas terras sese à suis subditis abstrahi viderent.
units.tr: 5. Indeed, in such great upheaval of all affairs, nothing more grievous or difficult could have happened to pious princes at that time than to see themselves drawn so far away from their subjects, into distant lands.

units.la: 6. Summa etiam fuit illic sententiarum servitus; quia omnes omnino & singuli fuerunt pontifici juramento obstricti, de quo diximus paulo antè; contrà autem in conciliis omnino liberæ esse debent episcoporum sententiæ. Hæc autem est juramenti pontificii summa, se (Romanos episcopos & clerum) defensuros statum pontificium, & regalia s.Pe-tri contra omnes homines, & con-servaservaturos auctoritatem, privilegia, & libertatem Romanæ ecclesiæ, & domini papæ pro summis viribus; e-aque dicturos, suasuros, & facturos in conciliis sedulò, quæ domino papæ placeant, & ad amplificandam ejus potentiam pertinere videatur. Quæ, quæso, major servitus excogitari potest?
units.tr: 6. There was also the utmost servitude of opinion there, because all and each one were bound to the pope by the oath of which we spoke a little earlier. On the other hand, in councils the opinions of bishops ought to be wholly free. Now the sum of the papal oath is this: they (the Roman bishops and clergy) will defend the papal state and the regalia of St Peter against all men, and will preserve the authority, privileges and liberty of the Roman Church and of the lord pope with all their strength; and they will diligently say, advise and do in councils whatever pleases the lord pope and seems to pertain to the enlargement of his power. What greater servitude, I ask, can be imagined?

units.la: 7. Præterea sententia condemnatoria jam tum lata erat in protestantes, priusquam vel concilium ipsum fuisset congregatum: sicuti constat ex bullâ Leonis X. quæ posteà acta à Paulo III. & IV.[?] pontificibus fuit confirmata, in quâ simpliciter confessio Augustana pro hæreticâ damnatur. Similiter Paulus III acerbè satis accusavit Carolum V. Imperatorem, quòd mitius cum protestatibus ageret. Constat etiam, quàm crudelissimis suppliciis sævitum sit multis in locis ex edictis pontificum in homines innocentes, propter veritatis divinæ professionem, in Hispaniâ, Galliâ, Angliâ, inferioribus partipartibus Germaniæ, & alibi: in libe-ro autem concilio omnia reservari debent legitimæ cognitioni.
units.tr: 7. Moreover, a sentence of condemnation against the Protestants had already been pronounced before the council itself was even convened, as is clear from the bull of Leo X, which was afterwards confirmed by the popes Paul III and IV[?], and in which the Augsburg Confession is simply condemned as heretical. Likewise Paul III quite bitterly accused the Emperor Charles V of dealing too leniently with the Protestants. It is also well known with what most cruel punishments, by papal edicts, innocent men were treated in many places for professing divine truth: in Spain, France, England, the lower parts of Germany and elsewhere. But in a free council all such matters ought to be reserved for lawful examination.

units.la: 8. Canones & decreta con-cilii istius Tridentini si ad scri-pturæ s.normam examinentur, com-perics[?] ea cum prophetarum & apo-stolorū scriptis manifestè, atq; è dia-metro pugnare, & religione Christiana desissimis[?] tenebris involvere: constitutiones item videbis inutiles, ineptas, superstitiosas, & tales quib. homines ad idololatriam & hypo-crisin facile abuti possint. Omitto autem multitudinem cerimoniarum, & similium rerum, quibus puritas doctrinæ Christianæ multis modis obscuratur. Item tyrannica illa; ut omnes & singuli sine examine, sine inquisitione & dijudicatione simpliciter assentiantur nudis concilii decretis: quodque nuda tā-tum ecclesiis decreta obtrudat sine rationibus; & contradicentibus, vel saltem inquirētibus anathema, ferrum & flammam proponat. de quo prolixius differendi dabitur com-modior locus aliàs.
units.tr: 8. If the canons and decrees of this Council of Trent are examined by the standard of Holy Scripture, you will find that they clearly and diametrically clash with the writings of the prophets and apostles, and wrap the Christian religion in the thickest darkness. You will likewise see the constitutions to be useless, foolish, superstitious, and of a kind by which men can easily be led into idolatry and hypocrisy. I pass over the multitude of ceremonies and similar things by which the purity of Christian doctrine is obscured in many ways. Likewise that tyrannical demand that all and each should simply assent to the bare decrees of the council without examination, without inquiry and without judgment; and that it thrusts bare decrees upon the churches without reasons, and holds out anathema, the sword and the flames to those who contradict or at least ask questions. On this matter a more suitable place for a fuller discussion will be given elsewhere.

units.la: 9. Denique quæ sint istius Tridentini, reliquorumque pontificiorum conciliorum effecta, liquet ex ante dictis: videlicet, multorum regnorum & status politici concus-sio, ruina & vastitas, discordiæ, tu-multus, bella cruentissima, & lanie-næ inter principes & alios viros bo-nos variæ.
units.tr: 9. Finally, what the effects of this Council of Trent and of the other papal councils have been is clear from what was said before: namely, the shaking, ruin and devastation of many kingdoms and political states, discords, tumults, most bloody wars, and various butcheries among princes and other good men.

units.la: Itaque quâ quæso conscientia possent viri pii, tum principes tum populus Christianus, ejusmodi concilium pro vero & legitimo agno-scere & probare?
units.tr: Therefore, I ask, with what conscience could pious men, both princes and the Christian people, acknowledge and approve such a council as true and lawful?

units.la: Convenit praxis ecclesiæ primitivæ: atque idem profitentur patres. Ita testa-tur ecclesiastica historia, 1. ad concilium œcumenicum accessisse non tantùm episcopos & clericos, verùm etiam laicos & politicos ex omnium ordinum hominibus. Ita in actis synodi Carthaginensis, cui præfuit Cyprianus, expressa mentio fit plebis: verba synodi hæc sunt. Quum in unum Carthagini convenissent calendis septembribus episcopi plu-rimi ex provinciâ Africâ, Numidi-ca, Mauritania, cum presbyteris & diaconis, præsente etiā plebis ma-ximâ parte, & lectæ essent literę Ju-bajani &c.
units.tr: The practice of the primitive Church agrees, and the Fathers profess the same. Thus ecclesiastical history testifies that: 1. to the ecumenical council there came not only bishops and clergy but also laymen and magistrates from every rank of men. Thus in the acts of the Synod of Carthage, over which Cyprian presided, express mention is made of the people. The words of the synod are these: when the bishops of many provinces of Africa, Numidia and Mauretania had assembled at Carthage on the first of September, together with presbyters and deacons, the greater part of the people being present as well, and the letters of Jubajanus etc. had been read.

units.la: 2. De superioritate non minus testatur historia ecclesiastica, & docet, quòd, quoties cunque de religione inciderunt controversiæ, nō ab episcopis vel papa Romano, sed vel ab imperatore solo, vel adhibitis etiā aliis Christiani orbis principi-bus, cōcilia sint decreta, & dissidē-tes convocati.
units.tr: 2. Ecclesiastical history bears no less witness concerning superiority, and teaches that whenever controversies about religion arose, councils were decreed and the dissenters summoned not by the bishops or the Roman pope, but either by the emperor alone or with other princes of the Christian world also taking part.

units.la: Ita synodum Niceñam convoca-vit Constantinus Imperator apud Euseb.l.1.cap.6.Rufin.lib.10. Constan-tinopolitanam Theodosius Major Sozom.l.7.cap.7. Ephesinam Theo-dosius Minor Euagr.lib.1.cap.3. Chal-cedonensem, quę item fuit una ex quatuor celeberrimis Martianus. Rursus Constantinopolitanam Ju-stinianus. Similiter dicuntur s, pa-tres tres de observatione legis catholicæ tractaturi cõvenisse in Aurelianensem urbem ex præceptione gloriosissimorum regum. quod fuit cõ, cilium Aurelianense secundum, & provinciale. Similia leguntur de a-liis synodis veterum.
units.tr: Thus the Emperor Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea, see Eusebius, bk. 1, ch. 6; Rufinus, bk. 10. Theodosius the Great convened the Council of Constantinople, Sozomen, bk. 7, ch. 7. Theodosius the Younger convened the Council of Ephesus, Evagrius, bk. 1, ch. 3. Marcian convened the Council of Chalcedon, which is likewise one of the four most famous. Again, Justinian convened the Council of Constantinople. Similarly, three fathers are said to have assembled in the city of Orléans, to treat of the observance of Catholic law, by the command of the most glorious kings; this was the Second Council of Orléans, a provincial one. Similar things are read of other synods of the ancients.

units.la: Exstat etiam lex Justinianea No-vella 123. Ut omnibus modis in qua-que provincia annuæ synodi celebrentur: utque ad imperatorem i-psum deferantur, si qui viderentur negligentiores. Plura pete ex loco de Magistratu politico.
units.tr: There also exists a law of Justinian, Novella 123, that annual synods be held in every province by all means, and that they be reported to the emperor himself if any should seem negligent. Seek more on this in the place about the political magistrate.

units.la: 3. Similiter decreta fecerunt in conciliis primitivæ ecclesiæ nõ jux-ta pluralitatem suffragiorum, sed secundum sententiam eorum qui meliore s.[?] literarum fundamento niterentur.
units.tr: 3. Likewise, in the councils of the primitive Church they made decrees not according to the majority of votes, but according to the opinion of those who were better grounded in letters.

units.la: 4. Neque tantum episcopos; ve-rum etiam alios viros pios & doctos ad decisiones & decreta facienda ad-hibuerunt. Ita interventu unius Paphnutii in concilio Niceno de-sensum est sacerdotum conjugium,
units.tr: 4. They admitted to the making of decisions and decrees not only bishops but also other pious and learned men. Thus, through the intervention of one man, Paphnutius, at the Council of Nicaea, the marriage of priests was defended,

units.la: cujus usum interdixerant reliqui patres & episcopi quorum trecenti & octodecim fuerunt. In ejusdem synodi historia legitur, senem quendam laicum non ita philosophiæ peritū plus præstitisse adversus philosophos, quàm cæteri episcopi omnes.qua de re vide Sozomenū hist.lib.1. & Ruffin.lib.1.
units.tr: whose use the other fathers and bishops, of whom there were three hundred and eighteen, had forbidden. In the history of the same synod it is read that a certain old layman, not very skilled in philosophy, achieved more against the philosophers than all the other bishops. On this matter see Sozomen, Hist. bk. 1, and Rufinus, bk. 1.

units.la: 5. Exstant etiam exempla piorū patrum, qui detrectarunt illas synodos, in quibus idololatriam & tyrannidem stabiliri animadverterunt. Ita, quum Constantinus Imperator in Tyrum concilium congregasset, Athanasius confestim noctu ex urbe discessit, posteaquam videlicet animadvertisset præcipuos concilii indicti viros non obscure cum Ario ludere simulque subordinatos esse calumniatores, à quibus falsò esset accusandus. Similiter Maximus, episcopus Hierosolymitanus noluit accedere ad synodum Antiochenam, imperatore Constantino congregatam, quum animadverterer, animam Constantini. Arianorum fraude jam esse seductam. Idem le-gitur de aliis viris pijs & doctis, quòd discesserint è concilijs post-ea quam animadvertissent homines hæreticos cum suo satellitio insidio-sa consilia tractare. Item de Chryso-stomo, qui recusavit adire synodum adversus se indictam; & alij.
units.tr: 5. There are also examples of pious fathers who refused to attend those synods in which they perceived idolatry and tyranny being established. Thus, when the Emperor Constantine had summoned a council to Tyre, Athanasius at once left the city by night, after he had clearly perceived that the leading men of the council that had been convened were openly playing with Arius, and that accusers subordinate to them were ready to accuse him falsely. Likewise Maximus, bishop of Jerusalem, refused to come to the Synod of Antioch, which had been called by the Emperor Constantine, when he saw that the soul of Constantine had already been seduced by the deceit of the Arians. The same is read of other pious and learned men, who withdrew from councils after they had perceived heretical men treacherously plotting with their band of henchmen. So too of Chrysostom, who refused to go to the synod summoned against him, and others.

units.la: Ambrosius in 1. Timoth. 5 scribit, in primitiva ecclesia hoc observatum fuisse, ut certus esset numerus virorum ætate & rerum prudentia gravium ex populo constitutus, sine quorum consilio nihil fieret in ecclesia, quod arduum esset, & diligentiore aliquâ deliberatione indigeret: deinde conqueritur, illud præclarum institutum postea paulatim concidisse, non sine magno ecclesiæ incommodo.
units.tr: Ambrose, in his commentary on 1 Timothy 5, writes that in the primitive Church this was observed: a fixed number of men from the people, grave in age and in practical wisdom, was constituted, and without their counsel nothing was done in the Church that was difficult and needed some more careful deliberation. He then laments that this excellent institution gradually fell into decay afterwards, not without great inconvenience to the Church.

units.la: Augustinus epist. 48. & 162. & 166. et pluribus in locis testatur, reges & politicos magistratus de rebus divinis & dogmatibus in ecclesia controversias cognovisse & dijudicasse. Item lib. 3. ca.17. allegat exemplum Constantini, & refert verba ex literis ejus ad alium vicarium, ubi Constantinus testatur se inter partes cognovisse & innocentem Coelianū comperisse. Idē Augustinus in opere breviculo collationum cum Donatistis, sub initiū et finem, di-cit; quòd catholici episcopi & Donatistæ, jussu imperatoris inter se gestis apud tribunum & notarium Marcellinum habitis contulerint: diserte item ꝓfitetur[?], quòd ingres-sis utrisq; partibus, primo loco re-citatum sit rescriptū Imperatoris, quo jussit collationē inter episcopos fieri: deinde secundo loco etiam recitatum sit edictum ipsius cognitoris, quod per provinciam miserat, ut convenirent utriusq; partis episcopi, & intra diem calendarum Juniarū conferendi causa congregarentur Carthagine. Præterea dicit, quòd ex consilio & moderamine Marcellini omnia fuerint in-stituta & gesta; quod idem ille sæpius fuerit interlocutus;& denique audita, quantum satis erat, utraque parte, sententiam tulerit hanc: Donatistas à catholicis omnium documentorum manifestatione confutatos esse.
units.tr: Augustine, letters 48, 162 and 166, and in many other places, testifies that kings and civil magistrates took cognizance of and judged controversies about divine matters and doctrines in the Church. Likewise in book 3, chapter 17, he cites the example of Constantine and quotes the words of his letter to another vicar, where Constantine declares that he had heard the parties and found Caecilian innocent. The same Augustine, in his short work on the conference with the Donatists, says at the beginning and at the end that the Catholic bishops and the Donatists held a conference by order of the emperor, in proceedings conducted before the tribune and notary Marcellinus. He also clearly states that when both parties had entered, first the emperor's rescript was read, by which he ordered that a conference be held between the bishops, and secondly the edict of the presiding judge himself was read, which he had sent throughout the province, that the bishops of both parties should meet and gather at Carthage for the purpose of conferring by the day of the Kalends of June. He adds that everything was arranged and carried out by the counsel and direction of Marcellinus, who often took part in the discussion; and finally, when both sides had been heard as far as was sufficient, he pronounced this sentence: that the Donatists had been refuted by the Catholics through the manifestation of all the documents.

units.la: Eusebius historiae tripartit. lib. 2. c. 11. testatur, Constantinum imperatorem in concilio Niceno primum sententiam suam dixisse: inq; eam omnes consentire & subscribere præcepisse.
units.tr: Eusebius, Historia tripartita, book 2, chapter 11, testifies that the emperor Constantine was the first to give his opinion at the Council of Nicaea, and that he ordered all to agree with it and to subscribe.

units.la: Apud Sozomenum idem ille Constantinus imperator dicitur episcopis mandasse, ut de cōtroversiis articulis inter se placidè deliberarent &c.
units.tr: In Sozomen, the same emperor Constantine is said to have charged the bishops that they should deliberate calmly among themselves about the controverted articles, etc.

units.la: Apud Theodoretum lib. 1 cap. 12, legitur præterea, quòd Constantinus ille subscripserit symbolum synodi Nicenæ. Deinde in principio epistolæ ejus hæc verba recitantur. Plurimis collectis episcopis, me quoq;, taquā e numero vestrò, præsente, de omnibus conveniente inquisitione tractatum fuit: minimè enim negaverim, quo maximè gaudeam, esse me in societate ministerii vestri.
units.tr: In Theodoret, book 1, chapter 12, it is further read that this Constantine subscribed the creed of the Nicene synod. Then at the beginning of his letter these words are quoted: "When many bishops had been gathered, and I too was present as one of your number, the matter was discussed and examined in full; for I would by no means deny, which gives me the greatest joy, that I am in the fellowship of your ministry."

units.la: De libertate cōciliorum nota est sententia Cypriani. Liberæ esse debent, inquit, episcoporum sententiæ, nec quisquam diversè sentientem condemnet, nec enim quisquā no-strum episcopum sc.[?] episcoporum esse constituit, aut tyrannico terro-re ad obsequendi necessitatem col-legas suos adigit: quilibet enim habet potestatem & arbitrium li-berum.
units.tr: The saying of Cyprian on the freedom of councils is well known: "The opinions of bishops ought to be free," he says, "nor should anyone condemn one who thinks differently; for none of us makes himself bishop of bishops, or by tyrannical terror compels his colleagues to the necessity of obedience; for each has his own power and free judgment."

units.la: 7. De præside & norma conci-liorū idem Cyprianus præclarè docet lib. 2. epist. ad Cælium epist. 3. Si sacerdotes Dei & Christi sumus, non invenio, quem magis sequi, quàm Deum & Christum, debeamus, quum ipse in euangelio maximè dicat: Ego sum lumen mundi, qui me sequutus fuerit, non ambulabit in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitæ, nec ergo in tenebris ambulemus, Christum sequi & præcepta ejus servare debemus. Idē prorsus docet Augustinus libr. de unitate ecclesiæ. ecclesiæ cap. 3. Sed, vt dicere cœperam, non audiamus, hæc dicis, sed audiamus, hæc dicit Dominus; sunt libri dominici quorum auctoritati vtriq; consentimus, vtriq; credimus, vtriq; seruimus: ibi quæramus ecclesiam, ibi discutiamus causam nostram. plura pete ex loco de f. scriptura.
units.tr: 7. On the president and rule of councils, Cyprian himself teaches admirably, book 2, letter 3, to Caecilius: "If we are priests of God and Christ, I do not find whom we ought to follow more than God and Christ, since he himself says most plainly in the Gospel: 'I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.' Therefore let us not walk in darkness, but let us follow Christ and keep his precepts." Augustine teaches exactly the same in his book on the unity of the Church, chapter 3: "But, as I had begun to say, let us not listen to what you say, but let us listen to what the Lord says. There are the books of the Lord, whose authority we both accept, in which we both believe and which we both serve; there let us seek the Church, there let us discuss our cause." Seek more on this from the place on Scripture's sufficiency.

units.la: Reliquum est vt pro ratione instituti nostri testimonia pontificiorum inquiramus.
units.tr: It remains that, in keeping with the purpose of our work, we examine the testimonies of the Papists.

units.la: 1. Superioritatem pontificis quod attinet, statuitur disertis verbis in de-cretis Gratiani c. Si papa. distinct. 40. papam in crimine hæresis (hoc est, vbi ipse de falsa doctrina fit arguendus) non esse judicem, sed ab aliis judicari debere.
units.tr: 1. As far as the superiority of the pontiff is concerned, it is laid down in express words in the Decretum of Gratian, c. Si papa, distinction 40, that the pope cannot be the judge in a charge of heresy (that is, where he himself is to be accused of false doctrine), but must be judged by others.

units.la: 2. De præside concilii nominatim etiam definiunt canones juris pontificii, principes debere adesse & præesse conciliis. vide ca. Principes. 2.3.4.5. & glossa addit, hoc tum vel præcipue locum habere, quum clerici fidem Christianam evertere nitantur, inq; eam sententiam allegat multos canones. Ibidem multis in locis legitur, reges & imperatores nō tantum interfuisse, sed etiam praefu-isse conciliis. vide ca. Adrianus 2. dist. 63. ca. ubinam. dist. 96. & similes.
units.tr: 2. Concerning the president of a council, the canons of the pontifical law also define by name that princes ought to be present at councils and to preside over them. See the chapter Principes, sections 2, 3, 4 and 5; and the gloss adds that this holds especially when the clergy strive to subvert the Christian faith, and it cites many canons to that effect. In the same place it is read in many passages that kings and emperors not only took part in councils but also presided over them. See the chapter Adrianus 2, distinction 63; the chapter Ubinam, distinction 96; and similar passages.

units.la: Idem fatetur Bellarminus lib. 1. de concilijs c.13.§. Habemus ergo, quod prima illa concilia etiam ab impe-rarorib.[?] indicta fuerint. Item, Quòd tunc lex imperialis prohibuit, ne frequentes conventus fierent sine imperatoris consensu. Item, Quòd eo tempore pontifex subiecerit se imperatoribus in temporalibus, & ideo non potuerit invito imperatore aliquid agere: idcirco etiam supplicaverit imperatori, ut juberet convocari synodum. Et cap. 5 ait, in secundo concilio generali omnino non interfuisse pontificem, nec per se nec per alium. & cap. 19. eum in nullis conciliis Orientalibus interfuisse dicit: & lib. 2. de Romano pontif. cap. 17. in Chalcedonensi, nec quidem per legatos adfuisse.
units.tr: Bellarmine too admits the same, book 1 on councils, chapter 13, section: "We have, therefore, that those first councils were also convened by the emperors." Likewise: "that then imperial law forbade frequent assemblies to be held without the emperor's consent." Likewise: "that at that time the pontiff submitted himself to the emperors in temporal matters, and therefore could not act against the emperor's will; for this reason he also begged the emperor to order a synod to be convened." And in chapter 5 he says that the pontiff was not present at all at the second general council, neither in person nor through another. And in chapter 19 he says that he was present at no Eastern councils; and book 2 on the Roman pontiff, chapter 17, that at Chalcedon he was not even present through legates.

units.la: Cusanus cardinalis lib. 2. de coExillo, inquit, tempore, quo imperatores coeperunt Christiani esse, ecclesiæ negocia ex illorum nutu pendere visa sunt, atque adeo maxima concilia de eorum sententia convocabantur: Item. Octo prima concilia generalia ab imperatoribus erat collecta, & pontifex Romanus ad instar aliorum patriarcharum sacras jussiones pro veniendo aut mittendo ad concilia recepit.
units.tr: Cusanus, the cardinal, book 2 on [the councils]: "At that time, when the emperors began to be Christians, the affairs of the Church seemed to depend on their nod, and indeed the greatest councils were convened by their judgment." Likewise: "The eight first general councils were gathered by the emperors, and the Roman pontiff, like the other patriarchs, received sacred summonses to come to or send to the councils."

units.la: His adde Franciscum de Victoria tract. de pontifice. Relect. 4. prop. 24. Audi, inquit, quid Johannes de Turrecremata cardinalis tenet, assertor vehementissimus pōtificiæ dignitatis, lib. 3. cap. 10. ubi loquens de utilitate conciliorum; celebratio, inquit, conciliorum utilis est, ad refræнandum exorbitantias quorundam pontificum, qui pontificatum suum aut extra patrum regulas pro voluntate sua exercent, aut simoniacâ pravitate dehonestât, aut vitâ scandalosâ cōfundunt: hac de causa
units.tr: To these add Francisco de Victoria, treatise on the pontiff, Relection 4, proposition 24. "Hear," he says, "what John of Torquemada, the cardinal, most vehement champion of papal dignity, holds, book 3, chapter 10, where, speaking of the usefulness of councils: The holding of councils is useful for restraining the excesses of certain pontiffs, who exercise their pontificate either outside the rules of the Fathers, at their own will, or dishonour it by simoniacal wickedness, or confound it by a scandalous life; for this reason"

units.la: [Right page, cropped strip, margin fragments only, not legible enough to transcribe reliably: "causa", "legi", "concilium", "ratorem", "Turrecre", "papæ hoc", "cardinalis", "consilio", "in defensione", "debere inte", "dilis", "Definitionem", "concilio", "vocant" — [illegible, ~120 letters]] causa legitur congregatum fuisse concilium Italiae, Romae per imperatorem, contra Johannem xxii. pa-pam, qui venator lubricus & incor-rigibilis erat: quod factum laudat Turrecremata. Item propter injus-tas dispensationes, & mandata in-solentia possunt convocari concilia generalia contra voluntatem papae: hoc quoque tenet Sylvester & cardinalis Turrecremata.
units.tr: [Right-hand page, cropped strip: only margin fragments survive, not legible enough to transcribe reliably.] For this reason it is read that a council of Italy was assembled at Rome by the emperor against John XXII, a slippery and incorrigible hunter (?) of the papacy, which deed Torquemada praises. Likewise, on account of unjust dispensations and insolent commands, general councils may be convened against the will of the pope; this too is held by Sylvester and the cardinal Torquemada.

units.la: 3. De membris conciliorum; consule Marsilium Patavinum, qui in defensione pacis, part. 2. cap. 20. & alibi defendit laicos idoneos etiam debere interesse ecclesiasticis co-ciliis. Idem etiam tuetur Panormi-tanus in quaest. 1. num. 26. & Petrus de monte, Venetus in tractatu de concilio quaest. 3. num. 7. & alii.
units.tr: 3. On the members of councils, consult Marsilius of Padua, who in the Defensor pacis, part 2, chapter 20, and elsewhere, defends that suitable laymen too ought to take part in ecclesiastical councils. Panormitanus also upholds the same, on question 1, number 26, and Peter of Monte, the Venetian, in his treatise on councils, question 3, number 7, and others.

units.la: 4. De suffragatoribus praeterea Marsilius Patavinus lib. 2. cap. 21. demonstrat copiose ex vetustis conciliis, in concilio principibus compete-re non tantum suffragiorum, &, ut vocant, consultandi vocem, verum etiam definiendi ac determinandi ius ac potestatem.
units.tr: 4. Moreover, concerning those who give votes, Marsilius of Padua, book 2, chapter 21, shows at length from ancient councils that in a council the princes possess not only the right of voting and of giving, as they call it, counsel, but also the right and power of defining and determining.

units.la: §. De auctoritate suffragiorum do-ctorum Gerson part. 1. de examin. doctrina-rum. Et prima, inquit, veritas haec stat, quod scilicet aliquis simplex non auctorisatus, possit tam excellenter in s. literis esse eruditus, ut ejus assertioni plus sit credendum in casu doctrinali, quam papae declarationi. His convenit illud Panormitani in c. significasti, de elect. ubi ita concludit, quod in concernentibus fidem di-ctum unius privati melioribus auctoritatibus veteris aut novi testamenti submixtum, quam papae dicto, praeferendum etiam sit papae dicto. Item Picus Mirandula, de quaest. An papa sit supra concilium. ait, quod simpli-ci rustico & infanti & anicula plus credendum sit, quam pontifici ma-ximo & mille ejus episcopis, si hi co-tra euangelium, isti autem pro eua-gelio verba facerent.
units.tr: §. On the authority of the votes of learned men: Gerson, part 1, On the examination of doctrines. "And the first truth," he says, "is this: that some unordained layman may be so excellently learned in the Holy Scriptures that, in a matter of doctrine, his assertion is to be believed more than the declaration of the pope." To this agrees that saying of Panormitanus on the chapter Significasti, On elections, where he concludes that in matters concerning faith, the word of a single private person, supported by better authorities of the Old or New Testament, is to be preferred even to the word of the pope. Likewise Pico della Mirandola, in the question Whether the pope is above a council, says that more credence is to be given to a simple peasant, a child, or an old woman than to the supreme pontiff and his thousand bishops, if the latter speak against the Gospel and the former speak for the Gospel.

units.la: Audi etiam Franciscum de-vict. in Relect. 4. Si bene revolvantur histo-riae, riæ, tempora antiquorum cōcilio-rum, reperiemus pontifices similes fuisse conciliorū patribus, nec præ-sumsisse decreta conciliorum tam facilè dispensare, sed tanquam di-vina oracula observare. Jam verò nec mala nostra nec remedia ferre possumus. & Joh.Ferum com.in act. 15.
units.tr: Hear also Franciscus de Victoria in his Relectio 4. If the histories are carefully turned over and the times of the ancient councils examined, we shall find that the popes were like the fathers of those councils, and did not presume to dispense so easily with the decrees of the councils, but kept them as divine oracles. Now, however, we can neither bear our evils nor find remedies for them. And Joannes Ferus on Acts 15.

units.la: Quum magna inquisitio esset: vide quam prudenter apostoli agunt, nō præcipitant sententiam in rebus fi-dei, non satis est dicere, volumus & mandamus. quid mirum, si in hoc concilio fuerit Spiritus s. Nos autē aliter cōvenimus cum magnâ pompâ, pollicemur nobis quidvis licere de plenitudine potestatis, quomodo Spiritus s. huiusmodi conventus probare possit?
units.tr: When there was a great inquiry, see how prudently the apostles act: they do not rush to judgment in matters of faith, and it is not enough to say, "We wish and command." What wonder if the Holy Spirit was present at that council? But we meet otherwise, with great pomp, and promise ourselves that we may do anything by the fullness of power. How could the Holy Spirit approve gatherings of this kind?

units.la: 6. De norma & regula cōtroversiarum Stapletonus præfat. in euangelistas Utinam, inquit, credendi forma a primæva peteretur ecclesia, quæ nullam regulam præter euangelium novit. Plura pete ex loco de verbo Dei.
units.tr: 6. On the norm and rule of controversies. Stapletonus, in the preface to the Gospels: Would that the form of belief were sought from the primitive Church, which knows no rule except the Gospel, he says. Seek more on this from the place concerning the Word of God.

units.la: 7. De loco hæc habet Text. in clemē-tina: tina Pastoralis, para. Num quid de sent. & rejudic. Num quid cōparere quis debet in loco multū potenti, & adversum se in odiū pvocato? & quis auderet: aut quâ ratione teneretur aliquis cōsistorii talis subire judicium? & se in hostiū sinū reponere, ac ad mortem, per violentā injuriā, nō per justitiā inferenda, ultro se offer-re? hæc quidē jure timentur, hæc de more vitantur, hæc humana fugit ratio, hæc abhorret natura: desperet ergo qui citationem hujusmodi saperet arctasse citatum.
units.tr: 7. On this point the Text in the Clementines, Pastoralis, para. Num quid, on sentence and rejudgment, says: Ought anyone to appear before a judge who is very powerful and stirred up to hatred against him? And who would dare, or on what ground would anyone be bound, to submit to the judgment of such a consistory, to place himself in the bosom of his enemies, and to offer himself willingly to death through violent wrong, not through justice? These things are rightly feared, these are avoided by custom, these the human mind shuns, these nature abhors. Let him therefore despair who thinks a summons of this kind has bound the summoned man.

units.la: Quæstio Secunda.
units.tr: Second Question.

units.la: An viri pii debeant moveri banno, excommunicatione, atq; anathematis, quæ papa Romanus & antistites concilii Tridentini vibrant in protestantes? Romani pontifici affirmant. Orthodoxi pro-testantes negant.
units.tr: Whether godly men ought to be moved by the ban, excommunication and anathema which the Roman Pope and the prelates of the Council of Trent hurl against the Protestants? The Roman pontiffs affirm. The orthodox Protestants deny.

units.la: Orthodoxa sententia probatur: Nam non sufficit excommunicare; sed tū demū excōmunicatio habetur rata apud Deū, si sit legitima: Ita Joh. 9. recepit Christus eū, quē ejecissent sacersacerdotes & pharisæi , propterea quia confessus esset Dominum. Similiter Johan. 16.2. prædicit Dominus discipulis, quòd movedi essent synagogis: quodq; venturum esset tempus, quum, quisquis eos interemerit, putet se cultū præstare Deo.
units.tr: The orthodox opinion is proved: For it is not enough to excommunicate; excommunication is held valid before God only if it is lawful. Thus in John 9 Christ received the man whom the priests and Pharisees had cast out, because he had confessed the Lord. Similarly in John 16:2 the Lord foretold to his disciples that they would be put out of the synagogues, and that the time would come when whoever killed them would think he was offering service to God.

units.la: Si ergo valere debet & confirma-ri apud Deum excommunicatio, requiritur, ut instituatur ad exemplū apostoli 1.Cor.5.4. primum à veris Dei & Christi Jesu servis; secundò præeunte legitimâ cognitione; tertiò justis de causis: quartò ex præscriptis verbi Dei omniaq; instituâ-tur in timore & tremore Domini cū spiritu mansuetudinis & prudentiæ Christianæ.
units.tr: If therefore excommunication is to be valid and confirmed before God, it is required that it be instituted after the pattern of the apostle, 1 Cor. 5:4: first, by the true servants of God and of Jesus Christ; second, after lawful investigation; third, for just causes; fourth, according to the prescriptions of the Word of God; and all of it should be carried out in the fear and trembling of the Lord, with the spirit of gentleness and Christian prudence.

units.la: Deinde ut stringatur in apertos gloriæ & veritatis Dei hostes, homi-nes pertinaces, seductores, & in a-perte stagitiosos, eosque αὐτοκατα-κρίτως [?], sibi damnatos, omneq; Christiana admonitione spernentes, sicut liquet ex Matt.18.17.1.Cor.5.18.1. Thess.3.4.Tit.3.11.
units.tr: Furthermore, it is to be directed against open enemies of the glory and truth of God, obstinate men, seducers, and those who are openly shameless, who are self-condemned [αὐτοκατακρίτως] and reject every Christian admonition, as is clear from Matt. 18:17; 1 Cor. 5:11, 13; 1 Thess. 3:14; Titus 3:10–11.

units.la: At in concilio Tridentino excō- municatio atque anathemata sunt facta à judice incompetente. pōti- sex namq; Romanus ejusq; conju- rati grauissimorū criminū nomine à maximâ Christianitatis parte da- mnati, vel falsè accusati sunt & fue- runt: quia itaque de re & statu ipsius papatus agebatur, nulla nec ciuilis, nec naturalis ratio patitur eum sibi de re propriâ jus dicere.
units.tr: But at the Council of Trent the excommunication and anathemas were pronounced by an incompetent judge. For the Pope and his associates were condemned, or were falsely accused, by the greater part of Christendom on account of most grave crimes; and since the matter concerned the very state of the papacy itself, no civil or natural reason allows him to pronounce judgment in his own cause.

units.la: 2. Deinde falsi isti sacerdotes ju- diciū illud sibi sumserunt in prote- stantes inauditos atq; indicta causa.
units.tr: 2. Next, those false priests took to themselves that judgment against Protestants who were not heard and whose case had not been tried.

units.la: 3. Pro mera libidine sua , idque
units.tr: 3. Out of mere lust of their own; and that

units.la: 4. Propterea: quia idololatriæ ac tyrannidi Romanæ contradiceret, omnesq; de religione controversias ex præscripto verbi Dei dirimi vel- lent.
units.tr: 4. Because it would be contrary to the idolatry and Roman tyranny, and they wished all controversies about religion to be settled by the prescription of the Word of God.

units.la: Idem statuunt patres. Augustinus super Matthæum; Ridiculum est, ut eum mundum esse dicamus, qui à vincu- lis peccatorum suorum ligatus est, propter hoc solum, quod episcopus dicitur habere hujusmodi potestātem, ut soluti ab eo, soluti sint in cœ-lo: & ligati in terris, ligati sint in cœ-lo. sit ergo irreprehensibilis, qui al-terum ligat aut soluit. Item libr. contra Secundinum Manichæum cap.1. Senti de Augustino quicquid libet, sola me in oculis Dei conscientia non accu-sat. Hieronymus in Leviticu[?]. Si quis, in-quit, non recto judicio eorū, qui præ-sunt ecclesiæ, depellatur, & foras mittatur, si ipse non ante exiit, hoc est, si non ipse egit, ut mereretur exi-re, nihil læditur in eo, quòd non re-cto judicio ab hominib. videtur ex-pulsus, & ita fit, ut interdum ille, qui foras mittitur, intus sit, & ille foris, qui intus retineri videtur. Origenes su-per Leviticum, hom. 14. ad ca. 24. Quum aliquis exit a veritate, a timore Dei, a fide, a charitate, exit de castris ec-clesiæ, etsi per episcopi vocem mi-nimè abjiciatur: sicut è contrario, dum aliquis non recto judicio foras mittitur, scilicet si non ante exierit, id est, si non egerit, ut mereretur exire, nihil læditur.
units.tr: The Fathers hold the same. Augustine on Matthew: It is ridiculous to say that he is loosed who is bound by the chains of his own sins, merely because a bishop is said to have such power that those loosed by him are loosed in heaven, and those bound on earth are bound in heaven. Let him therefore be blameless who binds or looses another. Likewise in the book against Secundinus the Manichaean, chapter 1: Let people think of Augustine whatever they like; my conscience alone, before the eyes of God, does not accuse me. Jerome on Leviticus: If anyone, he says, is cast out and sent away by an unjust judgment of those who preside over the Church, and he himself did not first go out, that is, did not himself act so as to deserve to go out, nothing is harmed in him, even though he seems to men to have been expelled by an unjust judgment; and so it happens that sometimes he who is sent outside is within, and he who seems to be kept within is outside. Origen on Leviticus, homily 14 on chapter 24: When anyone departs from the truth, from the fear of God, from faith, from charity, he goes out of the camp of the Church, even if he is not cast out by the voice of the bishop; and conversely, when anyone is sent out by an unjust judgment, namely if he has not first gone out, that is, has not acted so as to deserve to go out, nothing is harmed.

units.la: Assentiuntur pontificii. Gratianus causa 24 quaest. 1 cap. Audivimus. Sin autem, inquit, ex corde suo novam haeresin confinxerit, ex quo talia praedicare coepit, neminem damnare potuit: quia non potest dejicere quemquam jam prostratus: ligandi namque vel solvendi potestas veris, non falsis sacerdotib. à Domino est tradita.
units.tr: The Papists agree. Gratian, Cause 24, question 1, chapter Audivimus: But if, he says, he has fashioned a new heresy from his own heart, from the time he began to preach such things he could condemn no one, because one who is already cast down cannot cast down another; for the power of binding and loosing has been given by the Lord to true priests, not false ones.

units.la: Lombardus lib. 4. sentent. distinct. 18, lit. H. Aliquando, inquit, sacerdotes ostendunt solutos vel ligatos qui ita non sunt apud Deum: & poenâ satisfactionis & excommunicationis interdum indignos ligant & solvunt, & indignos sacramentis admittunt, & dignos admitti arcent. Item paulo post, Quoscunq; ergo solvunt vel ligant, adhibentes clavem discretionis reorum meritis, solvuntur vel ligantur in coelis. &c. Item Quos ergo secundùm merita sententia eccle-siae percellit, laedit, & illi foris sunt apud Deum; qui autem non meruit, sententia ecclesiae non lae-ditur.
units.tr: Lombard, book 4 of the Sentences, distinction 18, letter H: Sometimes, he says, priests show as loosed or bound those who are not so before God; and sometimes they bind and loose with the penalty of satisfaction and excommunication those who are unworthy, and admit to the sacraments those who are unworthy, and keep away those who are worthy of admission. Likewise a little after: Therefore whomever they loose or bind, applying the key of discernment to the merits of the guilty, they are loosed or bound in heaven, etc. Likewise: Therefore whom the sentence of the Church strikes according to their merits, they are harmed, and they are outside before God; but whom it does not deserve, the sentence of the Church does not harm.

units.la: Præterea hoc etiam manifestum est ex veterum historiâ & praxi apostolicâ, quòd, licèt pastores primas semper habuerint partes circa censuras ecclesiasticas, ordinis causâ, easq; administrarint, tamen ex communicandi potestas nõ fuerit penes unum episcopum, vel Romanum vel alium; neque etiam penes paucos pastores; sed penes ecclesiam, ita, ut citra consensum ecclesiæ ac præcipuorum ejus membrorum pastores ad exclusionem non processerint. Ita Cyprianus scribit ad Cornelium episcopum Romanum, se multum apud plebē laborare, ut pax detur lapsis: Hancer[?]go si per se dare potuisset, non erat cur tantopere de persuadēda plebe laborasset. Qui plura desiderat, consulat locū de disciplina ecclesiastica. Vide item libellum, qui titulus Brutum fulmen. Inde edoceberis, Papam communi orthodoxorum consensu non tantum à maximâ Europæ parte, tanquam incogruum atque incompetentem judice esse rejcrejectū, verum etiā ab illis ecclesiis & nationibus, quæ in Africa, Ægyp-to, Syriā, Oriēte, Asiā, & Græcia nomen suum inter ecclesias Christia-nas profitentur: idque merito pro-pter multiplicem illius impietatem: quia divinum honorem sibi tribuit, & religionem Christianam multis modis corrumpit, imò verò sacrilegè illudit ac ridet; & contrà falsas & idololatricas religiones ecclesiis obtrudit, & tyrannicè in eas dominatur, majestates pedibus coculcat: communem pacem ac totum reipubl. Christianæ statum variis facti-onibus evertit: atque omnis generis fraudibus, dolis, mendaciis, perjuriis, minis, sævitiâ sedem suâ confirmat, sicuti ibidem prolixè demonstratur. Adde si vis reliquorum Canonistarum declaratione, & non minus appare-bit omnia pontif. Rom. fulmina esse injusta atq; irrita, ac proinde ipsam excommunicationis maledictione in illius atq; asseclarū caput redūdare[?]: quandoquidem neq; justa ex causa, neq; judiciali ordine servato est emissa.
units.tr: Moreover, this is also plain from the history of the ancients and from apostolic practice: although the ministers have always held the chief place in ecclesiastical censures, on account of their office, and have administered them, yet the power of excommunicating did not rest with one bishop, whether Roman or other, nor even with a few ministers, but with the Church; so that the ministers did not proceed to exclusion without the consent of the Church and of its leading members. So Cyprian writes to Cornelius, the Roman bishop, that he labours greatly among the people so that peace may be given to the lapsed; for if he could have given it by himself, there would have been no reason for him to labour so much to persuade the people. Let him who wants more consult the place on ecclesiastical discipline. See also the little book entitled Brutum fulmen. From it you will learn that the Pope has been rejected by the common consent of the orthodox, not only by the greater part of Europe as an unfit and incompetent judge, but also by those churches and nations which in Africa, Egypt, Syria, the East, Asia and Greece profess their name among the Christian churches; and this deservedly, on account of his manifold impiety: because he claims divine honour for himself and corrupts the Christian religion in many ways, indeed sacrilegiously mocks and laughs at it; and against the true religion he thrusts false and idolatrous religions upon the churches, and tyrannically lords it over them, trampling majesties underfoot; he overthrows the common peace and the whole state of the Christian commonwealth by various factions, and confirms his seat by every kind of fraud, trickery, lies, perjuries, threats and cruelty, as is demonstrated at length in the same place. Add, if you wish, the declarations of the remaining canonists, and it will be no less evident that all the thunderbolts of the Roman pontiff are unjust and void, and therefore that the curse of excommunication rebounds upon the head of him and of his followers, since it has been issued neither for a just cause nor after the judicial order has been observed.

units.la: REFUTATIO OBJECTI-ONUM PONTIFICIARUM AD asserendam concilii Tridentini & similium auctoritatem.
units.tr: A REFUTATION OF THE PAPISTS' OBJECTIONS IN DEFENCE OF THE AUTHORITY OF THE COUNCIL OF TRENT AND OF SIMILAR COUNCILS.

units.la: COacervant pontificii magnum numerum argumentorum, quibus causam & sedem suam confirmare conantur: & primum repetunt eadem fere, quae attigimus in Medulla Papismi, loco de conciliis.
units.tr: The Papists heap up a great number of arguments by which they try to confirm their cause and their seat. First they repeat almost the same things that we touched on in the Medulla Papismi, in the section on councils.

units.la: Deinde, quia, pro more suo, numero certant, plura objiciunt. Dominum abominari eos, qui discordiam serant inter fratres: tales autem esse, quotquot contradicunt concilii Tridentini decretis, ¶[?]. Imò verò tales sunt; quotquot concilii Tridentini & similium edictis subscribunt, quia nulla legitimi concilii forma illic cernitur, sicuti evidentissimis argumentis comprobavimus. Deinde nullam aliam ob causam doctores orthoorthodoxi Romanensium decretis se opponunt, quàm ut falsa doctrina & idololatriæ cultus è medio tollantur, neq; permittatur pontificum factionibus, ut pro suo libitu in clerum Domini tyrannidem exerceant: atq; ita nihil aliud spectat, quàm divini nominis gloriam ac christianæ reipub. salutem, quantum fieri potest, salvam atq; incolumem. 3: [?]Ut testari Dominum, quod, qui male agit, oderit lucem: ne arguantur opera ipsius. Idem autem cernit in Protestantibus: quia vocati ad concilium œcumenicum aliquoties, parere noluerunt, sed publica judicia subterfugerunt. Recusarunt Protestantes adire concilia satanica, impia, & quæ plena sunt insidiarum, nunquam vero ullum concilium libri, neq; etiam ullius pii atq; intelligentis judicium fugerunt; sed potius in publicis Imperii conventibus multis jam annis flagitarunt, ut quæ de religione est controversia, in publica synodo legitimè disceptaretur, cognosceretur, ac dijudicaretur. deinde, quia nondum hoc impetrari potuit. ediderunt fidei suæ confessione, eamq; in consessu totius Imperii cæsari & ordinibus obtulerunt. hoccine est fugere lucem & quærere latebras?
units.tr: Next, since they are keen on numbers, as is their custom, they raise more objections. The Lord abhors those who sow discord among brethren; but all who contradict the decrees of the Council of Trent are such. ¶[?]. Indeed, rather, all who subscribe to the edicts of the Council of Trent and similar bodies are such, since no form of a lawful council can be seen there, as we proved by the most evident arguments. Further, the orthodox teachers of the Romanists oppose the decrees for no other reason than that false doctrine and the worship of idols may be removed, and that the factions of the popes may not be permitted to exercise tyranny over the clergy of the Lord as they please. Thus their aim is nothing other than the glory of the divine name and, as far as possible, the safety and welfare of the Christian commonwealth. 3: [?]As the Lord bears witness that whoever does evil hates the light, lest his works be exposed. Now the same is seen in the Protestants, because, though called several times to an ecumenical council, they refused to attend, and shunned public judgments. The Protestants refused to go to councils that are satanic, impious, and full of snares; but they never fled from any council of a free and godly people, nor from the judgment of any pious and intelligent person. Rather, in the public assemblies of the Empire they have for many years demanded that the controversy about religion be lawfully debated, examined, and decided in a public synod. Since this could not yet be obtained, they published their confession of faith and presented it to the Emperor and the estates of the Empire, in the assembly of the whole Empire. Is this what fleeing the light and seeking hiding-places means?

units.la: Præterea ajunt: Publica auctoritate missos esse legatos & oratores, qui regibus & reliquis totius orbis christiani principibus concilium Tridentinum denunciarent et singulos ad illud vocarent. Idem etiam Protestantibus denunciatum esse, non tantum pontificis, verum etiam Imperatoris Romani, quem summum suum magistratum dicunt, auctoritate. Decuisse itaq; ut aut ipsi coram interfuissent concilio, aut suos legatos cum mandatis misissent. ⁑ Principes protestantes, istis legatis & oratoribus pontificum Romanorum abunde & graviter responderunt: deinde etiam recusationum suarum causas justissimas publicis scriptis ediderunt, atq; etiam majestati Imperatoriæ & statibus Imperii exhibuerunt, sicuti constat ex annalibus, diariis & actis Imperii. Lutherum & cateros Protestantium doctores arrepto calamo, omnium conciliorum auctoritatem abrupisse. ⁑ Non omnium,
units.tr: Moreover they say: Legates and envoys were sent with public authority to announce the Council of Trent to the kings and the other princes of the whole Christian world, and to summon each of them to it. The same was also announced to the Protestants, by the authority not only of the pope but also of the Roman Emperor, whom they call their supreme magistrate. Therefore they ought either to have been present at the council in person, or to have sent their own envoys with instructions. ⁑ The Protestant princes replied fully and weightily to these legates and envoys of the Roman popes. Then they also published in public writings the most just causes of their refusal, and presented them to the Imperial Majesty and the estates of the Empire, as is evident from the annals, diaries, and records of the Empire. Luther and the other teachers of the Protestants, taking up the pen, have destroyed the authority of all councils. ⁑ Not of all,

units.la: sed tantum Romanensium & hæreticorum: Imò verò hoc unicum doctores Protestantium efflagitant, ut concedatur concilium christianum liberum, legitimum, in quo veritatis eruendæ media neq; deserantur negligentius, neq; contemnatur fastidiosius. atq; hoc ipsum noverunt pontificiorum doctores. Bellarminus, lib. 1. de conc. c. 5. inquit Lutherani prima sex generalia concilia recipiunt & cap. 21. Lutherani concilia generalia efflagitant. Similiter Stapletonus de doct. princ. l. 10. c. 8. quatuor concilia generalia Calvinus dicit se, ut sacrosancta, revereri Audi etiam Calvinum in Institut. Nos, inquit ille liberter concedimus, si quo de dogmate incidat disputatio, nullum esse certius remedium, quàm si verorum episcoporum chorus conveniat, ubi controversum dogma excutiatur.
units.tr: but only of the Romanists and the heretics. Indeed, the only thing the teachers of the Protestants demand is that a free and lawful Christian council be granted, in which the means of bringing out the truth are neither neglected carelessly nor scorned disdainfully. The teachers of the Papists know this very well. Bellarmine, On Councils, book 1, chapter 5, says: The Lutherans accept the first six general councils; and chapter 21: The Lutherans demand general councils. Likewise Stapleton, On the Principles of Doctrine, book 10, chapter 8: Calvin says that he reveres the four general councils as holy. Hear also Calvin in the Institutes: We, he says, gladly grant that if a dispute arises about some doctrine, there is no surer remedy than for a company of true bishops to meet, where the disputed doctrine may be examined.

units.la: ⁵ Protestantes non posse pati judicia aliorum, neque perferre superiorum.
units.tr: ⁵ The Protestants cannot tolerate the judgments of others, nor bear with their superiors.

units.la: Resp. Ita verò consueverunt Romanenses recte dicta & facta orthodoxè sententium calumniari: at probent maledicta sua æquis judicibus, argumen-tis firmis & solidis. Plura pete ex proximè præcedentibus.
units.tr: Reply: The Romanists are accustomed to slander in this way the things rightly said and done by those who think orthodoxly. But let them prove their slanders before fair judges, with firm and solid arguments. Seek more on this from what was said immediately before.

units.la: 6 Protestantes sine ulla justa causa, & temere a communi consensu discessisse, atq; infinitas distractiones moliri. Iure, & urgête necessitate discesserunt Protestantes a sede Romana, ad Dei gloriam & salutem populi christiani promovendam, sicuti demonstravimus supra quæst. 1. de jure protestantium contra pontificem Romanum atque ejus imperium. 7. Historiæ et experientiam testari, quantas mutationes secum traxerit, con[?]tradictio et defectio protestantium. Resp. Id factum est hominum malevolorum culpa & similia experti sunt apostoli, Item Christus ipse, atq; alii doctores pii.
units.tr: 6 The Protestants departed from the common consent without any just cause and rashly, and they are stirring up endless divisions. The Protestants departed from the Roman see rightly, and under the pressure of necessity, to advance the glory of God and the salvation of the Christian people, as we demonstrated above in question 1, On the Right of the Protestants against the Roman Pontiff and his rule. 7. History and experience bear witness how many changes the contradiction and defection of the Protestants have brought with them. Reply: This came about through the fault of malicious men; and the apostles, likewise Christ himself, and other godly teachers experienced the same things.

units.la: Interea verò omni studio quærunt Protestantes orthodoxi, ut incorrupta euangelii doctrina populo Christiano ritè proponatur, & traditiones humanæ, quæ verbi divini lucem satis diu obscurarunt, abolentur, vel ad normam legis divinæ corrigantur. Summis etiam Protestantes objecusse periculum & se et populum suae fidei commissum, hoc uno nomine, ne parerent sedi Romanae. Resp. Id factum est, quia norunt, se Dei verbo debe-re summam fidem atq; obedientiam, & pro defensione veritatis etiā gravissima, si ita necessitas exigat, esse perferenda, ad imitationem veterum piorum, teste Historia sacra?9 Vete-rem et puriorem ecclesiam synodorum indictione, veluti praecipuo ad tollendas controversias remedio, usam fuisse : Itaque merito suspectum esse piis omnibus, quòd Protestantes parere noluerint concilio legitimè cogregato. Resp. Vetus ecclesia piarum synodorum indictione usa est ad tollendas controversias: At demonstravimus Tridentinū & cæ-tera Romanensium concilia inter pias & legitimas synodos recenseri non posse. Petierunt itaque Protestantes, atque etiam nunc petunt concilium legitimum: hoc si detur, ejus cognitioni se se, sicut decet pie subjiciunt. 10 Tridentinum illud esse ritè indictum à Pontifice Romano. Resp. At auctoritas conciliorum dependet à Dei verbo; & prolixiùs demonstra-vimus antea quòd Romanus ponti-sex nihil juris habeat in principes & populum Christianum. Item in Me-dulla Papismi, loco de pontifice Ro-mano, quòd nulla sit ejus in ecclesia Dei auctoritas, in definiendis fidei negociis &c. ¹¹ Tridentinum illud re-praesentasse ecclesiam Jesu Christi, atque hanc esse audiendam omnibus. Resp: Ab-fit, ecclesiam dicamus illorum, qui condunt leges adversus Christum, qui est verum & unicum caput eccle-siæ. Itaque falsis doctoribus no credimus, idque ad præscriptum Christi. ¹² Non esse contemnenda concilia in Christi nomine congregata etc. Tale autem fuisse Tridentinum. Resp. Non contemnimus concilia, sed ea sub Christo, non supra Christum collocamus, neque ulli concedimus potestatem definiendi aliquid contra scripturas S. Deinde Tridentinum illud non fuisse in Christi nomine congregatum, neque ad formam piarum synodorum institutum, probavimus antea.¹³ In conciliis præsidere Spi-ritum ritum Christi. Ergo etiam in Tridentino eundem esse agnoscendum. ¶. Non in omnibus praesidet spiritus Christi, quod demonstravimus in loco de conciliis, in Medulla papismi. Neutiquam vero auditus est Spiritus s. in Tridentino: quia in eo multa definita sunt contra Dei verbum: Spiritus s. autem non retractat verbum suum. His adde, quod multi jactent Spiritum s. falso: quodcunq; vero illi praeter euangelium sub titulo Spiritus praetendunt vel obtrudunt, ne credamus. Christus enim semper copulat Spiritum s. & verbum, neque ullis promittit Spiritu, nisi qui docent, audiunt, & amplectuntur euangelium Joh.14.26. & alibi. ¶ Tridentinos illos patres fuisse collectos in Christi nomine. ¶. Non colliguntur in nomine Christi, quos constat a Chri-sto & euangelio ejus esse separatos: tales autem sunt quotquota ponti-ficis Romani auctoritate dependet.
units.tr: Meanwhile the orthodox Protestants seek with all zeal that the uncorrupted doctrine of the gospel be properly set before the Christian people, and that human traditions, which have obscured the light of the divine Word long enough, be abolished or corrected by the rule of the divine law. The Protestants also objected to the danger, both to themselves and to the people committed to their faith, under this one name: that they should not obey the Roman see. Reply: This was done because they know that they owe the highest faith and obedience to the Word of God, and that for the defence of the truth, even most grievous things must be endured if necessity so requires, in imitation of the ancient godly men, as sacred history attests. The ancient and purer Church used the summoning of synods, as a chief remedy for ending controversies. Therefore it is rightly suspected by all the godly that the Protestants were unwilling to submit to a lawfully gathered council. Reply: The ancient Church used the summoning of godly synods to end controversies. But we have shown that the Council of Trent and the other councils of the Romanists cannot be counted among the godly and lawful synods. Therefore the Protestants have sought, and still seek, a lawful council; if this is granted, they submit themselves to its examination, as is fitting. 10 That Council of Trent was rightly summoned by the Roman Pontiff. Reply: But the authority of councils depends on the Word of God; and we have demonstrated at greater length before that the Roman pontiff has no right over princes and the Christian people.
