Likewise in the Medulla Papismi, in the section on the Roman pontiff, that he has no authority in the Church of God to define matters of faith, etc. ¹¹ That council represented the Church of Jesus Christ, and this is to be heard by all. Reply: Far be it that we should call it the Church of those who make laws against Christ, who is the true and only head of the Church. Therefore we do not believe false teachers, and this according to the precept of Christ. ¹² Councils gathered in the name of Christ are not to be despised, etc. Now the Council of Trent was such. Reply: We do not despise councils, but we place them under Christ, not above Christ, and we grant to none the power of defining anything against the holy Scriptures. Further, we have proved before that that Council of Trent was not gathered in the name of Christ, nor instituted according to the form of godly synods. ¹³ In councils the Spirit of Christ presides. Therefore the same Spirit is to be acknowledged also in Trent. ¶. The Spirit of Christ does not preside over all things, as we demonstrated in the section on councils in the Medulla Papismi. Yet the Holy Spirit was by no means heard at Trent, because in it many things were defined against the Word of God; but the Holy Spirit does not retract his Word. Add to this that many falsely boast of the Holy Spirit; whatever they put forward or force upon us beside the gospel under the title of the Spirit, we must not believe. For Christ always joins the Holy Spirit and the Word, and he promises the Spirit to none except those who teach, hear, and embrace the gospel, John 14:26, and elsewhere. ¶ Those fathers of Trent were gathered in the name of Christ. ¶. They are not gathered in the name of Christ who are known to be separated from Christ and his gospel; and such are all who depend on the authority of the Roman pontiff.

units.la: Idem illud tum per pontifices tum per ecclesiam esse approbatum. ¶. Non quae-cunq; per pontifices, & ecclesia sunt approapprobata, de fide esse cēsent[?]: multo minus quæ videntur Romanensibus. Similiter non licet ecclesiæ vel pontifici ultra præscriptum Domini nostri Iesu Christi aliquid tentare, statuere aut exigere in fidei negocio.
units.tr: That same thing was approved both by the popes and by the Church. ¶. Not everything approved by the popes and the Church is judged to be of faith, much less what seems so to the Romanists. Likewise it is not lawful for the Church or the pontiff to attempt, establish, or demand anything in a matter of faith beyond the prescription of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: 16 In ecclesia esse saluberrimam concilio-rum auctoritatem: nullum autem exstitisse hoc nostro seculo præter illud Tridentinum. Resp. Equidem magna est eorum auctoritas, si secundum scripturæ normam loquantur & iudicent: at non satis est nudus titulus: imo vero etiam sunt concilia malignantium. de quibus pf.22...&26...& alibi. 17 Synodum esse apertam Tridenti hoc fine, ut sublatis omnibus erroribus puritas ipsa evangelii in ecclesia conservaretur. Resp. Quid autem revera patres isti quæsiverint, acta concilii & exitus comprobarunt: videlicet ut stabiliretur sedes Romana. 18 Ad normam s. literarum patres illius concilii decreta instituisse. Resp. Imo vero præter & contra scripturam s. populo Christiano obtrudunt traditiones suas Romanenses, nenses; easque pari pietatis affectu ac reverentia suscipiendas & venerandas decreverunt, sicut scripturam ipsam. Deinde scripturā ipsam secundum sensum vel depravatione ecclesiæ suæ Romanæ explicari volunt. Hoccine est instituere omnia ad normam scripturæ propheticæ & apostolicæ?{9} Nullam affulgere reconciliationis spem inter partes dissentientes in orbe Christiano, si annihiletur vel extenuetur Tridentina synodi auctoritas. &c.[?] Ergo dicamus cum Augustino lib. 3. contra Maxim. cap.14. Neque ego hujus, neque tu illius auctoritate detineris; scripturarum auctoritatibus, non quorumcunque propriis, sed utrisque communibus testibus: res cum re, causa cum causâ, ratio cum ratione decertet.
units.tr: 16 That the authority of councils is most salutary in the Church, but that none has existed in this our century except the Council of Trent. Reply: Indeed their authority is great, if they speak and judge according to the rule of Scripture. But a bare title is not enough; there are even councils of evildoers, concerning which see Ps. 22 and 26 and elsewhere. 17 That the Synod was convened at Trent with this aim, that with all errors removed the purity of the gospel itself might be preserved in the Church. Reply: What those fathers actually sought, the acts of the council and its outcome have shown: namely, that the Roman see might be established. 18 That the fathers of that council drew up their decrees according to the norm of the holy letters. Reply: On the contrary, besides and against Holy Scripture they force their Roman traditions upon the Christian people, and they have decreed that these are to be received and venerated with the same devotion and reverence as Scripture itself. Then they want Scripture itself to be explained according to the sense of their Roman church, or its corruption. Is this what it means to order all things according to the norm of prophetic and apostolic Scripture? There is no glimmer of hope for reconciliation between the parties dissenting in the Christian world, if the authority of the Synod of Trent is annihilated or diminished, etc. Therefore let us say with Augustine, book 3 against Maximinus, chapter 14: "I am bound neither by the authority of this man nor you by that of that man; let the matter be decided by the authorities of the Scriptures, not by the private claims of anyone, but by witnesses common to both sides: thing against thing, cause against cause, reason against reason."

units.la: Praeterea confugiunt ad Patres. Resp. At neque nobis desunt Patrum suffragia, quæ notavimus supra: deinde, quanta sit eorum auctoritas docuimus in Medullâ Papismi in loco de Patribus.{20} Ajunt veteres Imperatores sub gravissimarum poenarum comminatione natione vetuisse, ea, quæ semel in concilijs decreta, in controversiam revocare: & no-tam esse Juris consultissimam Martiani Imp. constitutionem, injuriam fieri reverendis-simæ synodi judicio, si quis semel judicata ac recte disposita revolvere, & publicè dis-putare contenderit. Resp. Ita, si quis recte disposita in controversiam re-vocet, at Tridentinum oppugnatur, quia quæ illic judicata, non sunt re-ctè disposita, sed depravata præter & contra scripturam propheticam & apostolicam: quæ autem à veteri-bus conciliis ex scriptura sunt de-finita, ea Protestantes unanimi con-sensu amplectuntur, & privatim ac publicè profitentur: quin etiam hoc nomine Tridentino contradicunt, ut veterum conciliorum orthodo-xa doctrina & auctoritas salva ad posteros propagetur, atq; ecclesiæ libertas sua restituatur.
units.tr: Furthermore, they take refuge in the Fathers. Reply: But we too do not lack the support of the Fathers, which we noted above. Further, how great their authority is we have shown in our Medulla Papismi, in the place concerning the Fathers. They say that the ancient emperors, under threat of the most severe penalties, forbade that what had once been decreed in councils be called into question again; and that the constitution of the Emperor Martian is most learned in law, that it is an injury to the most reverend judgment of the synod if anyone tries to reopen what has been judged and rightly settled, and to dispute it publicly. Reply: Yes, if anyone calls into question what has been rightly settled. But Trent is assailed because what was judged there was not rightly settled, but corrupted, besides and against prophetic and apostolic Scripture. What the earlier councils defined from Scripture, however, the Protestants embrace with unanimous consent, and profess both privately and publicly. Indeed, on this very ground they oppose Trent, so that the orthodox doctrine and authority of the ancient councils may be preserved and handed down intact to posterity, and the liberty of the Church restored.

units.la: Postremò adversus argumenta Orthodoxorum regerunt. {a}Nullum unquam concilium œcumenicum sine con-sensu Romani pontificis congregatum esse. Resp. Non quæritur de consensu, sed de superioritate, quam dicūt; & probavimus antea, jus convocandi concilii fuisse penes Imperatorem in ecclesiâ veteri, atque etiam Papam Romanū tum supplicasse imperatoribus: nunc autem omnibus imperat: Concilium sine auctoritate Romani pontificis congregatum esse indignum concilii nomine: nam non esse in nomine Christi congregatum.
units.tr: Finally, they hurl back against the arguments of the Orthodox: {a}No ecumenical council has ever been convened without the consent of the Roman pontiff. Reply: The question is not about consent but about the superiority which they claim. We have proved above that in the ancient Church the right of convoking councils belonged to the Emperor, and that even the Roman pope then made supplication to the emperors; but now he commands all. A council convened without the authority of the Roman pontiff is unworthy of the name of council, for it has not been convened in the name of Christ.

units.la: Resp. Respondeo cum Cusano Cardin. libro 2. de concil. cathol. cap. 25. & aliis doctoribus pontificiis. Ergo octo prima concilia non fuerunt firma, quoniam per Imperatores congregata leguntur, & Romanus pontifex ad instar aliorū patriarcharum sacras jussiones pro veniendo aut mittendo ad concilia recepit. Deinde non æquipollent hæc duo: In nomine Christi, & in nomine vel auctoritate Papæ congregare concilium. Rectius igitur Arias Montanus in locum Matth. 18.20. in nomine Christi dicit significare in spiritum Christi. & Jansenius in concord. c.72. In nomine, inquit, id est propter causam aliquam ad me pertinentem. {23} Conditionem illam, quam Protestantes requirunt (ne pontifex Romanus ei præsit, utpote pars litigantium) esse iniquam: eam namque locum habere tantùm in hominibus privatis, non autem in principe supremo. Resp. Ejusmodi principatum scriptura s. Romano pontifici nullibi concedit, neque opus est, ut his diutius immoremur: & nota est illa Jureconsultorum regula, Judex in sua suorumve causâ nemo esse debet. {24} Pios veteres semper acquievisse pontificis Romani definitioni, neque ulla alia concilia agnovisse pro legitimis, quam quæ ipse approbasset. {¶} Consule historias & multò rectius edoceberis. Equidem posterioribus seculis episcopi Romani, homines vafri, variis artibus, fraude, dolo, minis, mendaciis dominatum & jurisdictionem universalem in ecclesias omnes quæsiverunt, tandem etiam, quod voluerunt, obtinuerũt; at quod initio vitiosum est, nullo temporis tractu convalescere potest, nulla item præscriptio, nulla cōfuetudo, licet inveterata, quicquam valet adversus expressum Dei verbum. Et nota est pueris illa in dubitata juris regula: Non posse malè fidei possessorem in æternum unquam præscribere. Mala etiam fides non solum ad annos centum, verum etiam ad multa annorum milia opponi potest. Constat autem ex historia ecclesiastica, quod non tantum sexillæ[?] œcumenicæ, verum etiam aliæ permultæ synodi in Africa, & in Græcia aliisque nationibus fuerint congregatæ sine præsentia & auctoritate Papæ Romani & legatorum ejus. Nota item est historia synodi Carthaginensis, cui interfuit Augustinus: in qua Cælestinus ad imitationem suorum antecessorum provocationes episcoporum sibi vindicare nitebatur, cum manifestâ synodi Nicenæ depravatione. Plura vide in locis de pontifice Romano & conciliis.
units.tr: Reply: I answer with Cusanus the cardinal, book 2 On the Catholic Council, chapter 25, and with other Papist teachers. Therefore the first eight councils were not valid, since they are read to have been convened by emperors, and the Roman pontiff received sacred commands, like the other patriarchs, to come to the councils or to send representatives. Further, these two things are not equivalent: to convene a council in the name of Christ, and to convene it in the name or authority of the Pope. Rather, Arias Montanus rightly says on Matt. 18:20 that "in the name of Christ" means in the Spirit of Christ; and Jansenius in the Concordance, chapter 72, says: "In name, that is, on account of some cause pertaining to me." That condition which the Protestants require, namely that the Roman pontiff not preside over the council as a party to the dispute, is unjust, for it applies only to private persons and not to a supreme prince. Reply: Holy Scripture nowhere grants such a principate to the Roman pontiff, and there is no need to dwell on this longer. The well-known rule of the jurists is that no one ought to be judge in his own cause or in the cause of his own people. The pious ancients always acquiesced in the definition of the Roman pontiff, and recognised no councils as lawful except those he had approved. Consult the histories, and you will be taught far more correctly. In later centuries, to be sure, the Roman bishops, crafty men, sought dominion and universal jurisdiction over all churches by various arts, fraud, deceit, threats and lies; and at last they obtained what they wanted. But what is vicious at the beginning can never gain strength through the passage of time, and neither prescription nor custom, however long established, avails anything against the express word of God. The rule of law familiar even to boys is well known: a possessor in bad faith can never acquire a prescriptive title, however long. Bad faith can be objected not only for a hundred years but for many thousands of years. Moreover, it is clear from ecclesiastical history that not only the six ecumenical councils, but very many other synods in Africa, in Greece and in other nations, were convened without the presence and authority of the Roman pope and his legates. The history of the Synod of Carthage, in which Augustine took part, is also well known: there Celestine, following the example of his predecessors, struggled to claim for himself appeals from bishops, with a manifest corruption of the Nicene Synod. See more in the places on the Roman pontiff and on councils.

units.la: 35 Multas controversias ex s. literis decidi non posse, neque etiam satis tuto ad præscriptum s. literarum examinari, quia scriptura ptura est multis in locis obscura, ambigua &c. Resp. Imò verò, quæcunque ad salutem & Dei gloriam sunt scitu necessaria, ex scripturis prophetiis,& apostolicis perspicuè ac solidè peti & demonstrari possunt. De quare vide plura in loco de scriptura s. & verbo Dei.{26} In generali synodo septima esse definitum, quòd traditiones nō scriptæ sint recipiendæ: quæ autem semel definita, non debere in dubium revocari. Resp. Responsum est antea, ea tantùm fidem promereri atque assensum, quæ sunt definita piè & rite ex scripturâ prophetica & apostolica. His adde Bernhardum, qui epist.95.
units.tr: 35 Many controversies cannot be decided from the holy letters, nor examined safely enough by the rule of the holy letters, because Scripture is obscure and ambiguous in many places, etc. Reply: On the contrary, whatever is necessary to know for salvation and the glory of God can be sought and clearly and soundly demonstrated from the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures. See more on this in the place concerning Holy Scripture and the Word of God. In the seventh general synod it was defined that unwritten traditions are to be received, and that what has once been defined ought not to be called into doubt. Reply: It has been answered before that only those things deserve faith and assent which have been piously and rightly defined from prophetic and apostolic Scripture. To these add Bernard, who in letter 95 says:

units.la: Ad illud, inquit, concilium toto desiderio feror, in quo traditiones nō obstinaciùs defensantur, nec superstitiosius.{27} Veteris ecclesiæ doctores solitos esse allegare consensum ecclesiæ & traditiones apostolicas, quæ exstant in primorum patrum scriptis. Ita Irenæum opposuisse Florino testimonium patrum, qui ipsum antecesserunt, & comprimis Polycarpi, qui fuerat discipulus Johannis Euangelistæ & auditor apostolorum. Similiter à Basilio al-legari legari Gregorium Neocæsariensem. Simi-lia posse proferri de aliis. Resp. Neque nos contemnimus patrum testimonia, sed tantum exigimus, ut ea subjiciantur auctoritati scripturæ sacrae neque illi majorem auctoritatem sibi deferri petunt. Neque enim, inquit Augustinus epist. 3. ad Fortunat, quorumlibet disputationes, quamvis catholicorum & laudatorum hominum velut scripturas canonicas habere debemus, ut nobis nō liceat salva honorificentia, quæ ipsis debetur hominibus, aliquid in eorū scriptis improbare atq; respuere; si forte invenerimus, quod aliter senserint, quàm veritas habet divino adjutorio vel ab aliis intellecta vel à nobis. Plura pete ex loco de Patribus.
units.tr: "To that council, he says, I am drawn with all my longing, in which traditions are not defended obstinately, nor superstitiously." The teachers of the ancient Church were accustomed to cite the consensus of the Church and the apostolic traditions which exist in the writings of the first fathers. Thus Irenaeus opposed to Florinus the testimony of the fathers who had gone before him, and especially of Polycarp, who had been a disciple of John the Evangelist and a hearer of the apostles. Similarly Basil cited Gregory of Neocaesarea. Similar things can be produced from others. Reply: We do not despise the testimonies of the Fathers; we only require that they be subjected to the authority of Holy Scripture, and they themselves do not seek a greater authority for themselves. For, says Augustine in letter 3 to Fortunatus, we ought not to hold the disputations of any men, however Catholic and praiseworthy, as if they were canonical Scripture, so that we may not, with the honour due to such men, reject and disapprove anything in their writings if we find that they thought otherwise than the truth, understood either by others or by us with divine help. Seek more from the place concerning the Fathers.

units.la: 28 Nisi juxta suffragiorum pluralitatem fit decidenda controversia, penitus tolli forma conciliorum. Resp. si vero plurimorum sententia semper valere debeat, aperta est janua hostibus Christi quidvis moliendi, & periit salus reipubl. Christianæ. Ita enim juxta plupluraritem[?] suffragiorum damnatus est Christus. Major pars concilii Niceni damnavit matrimonia ecclesiasticorum. Rectè itaque pronunciat Canus in loco theol. lib. 5. cap. penult. §. Verum. Nego, inquit, quum de fide agatur, plurimorum judicium nos sequi oportere. neque enim hic, ut in humanis judiciis, ea suffragiorum numero metimur. scimus enim frequenter usu venire, ut major pars vincat meliorem.
units.tr: 28 Unless the controversy is decided according to the plurality of votes, the form of councils is utterly abolished. Reply: But if the opinion of the majority were always to prevail, the door would be open for enemies of Christ to attempt anything, and the salvation of the Christian commonwealth would perish. Thus Christ was condemned by a majority vote. The majority of the Council of Nicaea condemned the marriages of ecclesiastics. Rightly, therefore, Canus pronounces in his theological place, book 5, the penultimate chapter, section "Verum": "I deny, he says, that when faith is at issue we ought to follow the judgment of the majority. For here, unlike in human judgments, we do not measure by the number of votes. For we know that it often happens in practice that the majority defeats the better side."

units.la: 29 Diploma securitatis & salvi conductus esse evulgatum, inq. eo fidem publicam omnibus etiam protestantium doctoribus esse promissam. ℞[?]. At juxta sensum & interpretationé[?] Romanensiū: Hæreticis non esse habendam fidem.
units.tr: 29 The safe-conduct and letter of security were published, and in it public faith was promised to all, including the teachers of the Protestants. Reply: But according to the sense and interpretation of the Romanists, faith is not to be kept with heretics.

units.la: 30 Tridentinum illud fuisse œcumenicum, & omnibus promiscuè licuisse accedere. ℞[?] Nominatur quidem œcumenicum in diplomate; at obscurè significatur, nullos esse admittendos præter cardinales, episcopos & cæteros pontifices juratos; propterea hæc verba adjecerūt in diplomate; Quibus jure, aut privilegio, aut more majomaiorum conciliis generalibus interesse & sententiâ dicere liceat. Ité manifestius illud apparet ex illis verbis in editâ bullâ indictionis.
units.tr: 30 That council of Trent was ecumenical, and everyone was freely permitted to attend. Reply: It is indeed called ecumenical in the diploma, but it is obscurely implied that none are to be admitted except cardinals, bishops and the other sworn prelates. For this reason they added these words to the diploma: "by which right, privilege, or custom of our ancestors it is permitted to attend general councils and to give a judgment." Likewise, this appears more plainly from those words in the published bull of indiction.

units.la: Quocirca venerabiles fratres nostros omnibus ex locis patriarchas, archiepiscopos, & dilectos filios, abbates, cæterosq;, quibus in generali concilio sedere, & sententiam dicere jure communi, vel ex privilegio, vel ex antiquâ consuetudine licet etc.
units.tr: Wherefore, our venerable brothers, the patriarchs and archbishops from all places, and our beloved sons, the abbots and others, who by common law, or by privilege, or by ancient custom are permitted to sit in a general council and to give their opinion, etc.

units.la: 3¹ Solis episcopis competere potestatem judicandi; & laicos esse docendos ab episcopis & clericis, teste Ambrosio. ¶. Solis quidem episcopis competit ministerium docendi verbum & administrandi sacramenta, in synodis etiâ inter primos habentur: at quæ in libero concilio decernuntur, quæq; universaliter ad omnes pertinet, ab illorum deliberatione & definitione laici pii & docti nullo jure arceri debent vel possunt. 3² Solos episcopos esse pastores: ac proinde illos solos habere jus suffragii decisivi ordinarie: Idq; affirmari ex Jer.3. (Dabo vobis pastores qui pascent scientiâ et doctrinâ) reliquos ergo laicos vel vel plebejos ad pastorum officia non esse admittendos.ꝛ Rectius statuit Alphonsus de Castro lib.1. adversus hæres. c. 6. omnes sacerdotes esse pastores.
units.tr: 31 Only bishops have the power of judging, and laymen are to be taught by bishops and clergy, as Ambrose testifies. Reply: Indeed, the ministry of teaching the Word and administering the sacraments belongs only to bishops, and in synods they are counted among the first. But what is decreed in a free council, and what pertains universally to all, the pious and learned laymen may not and cannot by any right be excluded from deliberating upon and defining. 32 Only bishops are pastors, and therefore they alone ordinarily have a decisive right of vote. This is affirmed from Jer. 3: "I will give you pastors who shall feed you with knowledge and doctrine." Therefore the remaining laymen, or commoners, are not to be admitted to the offices of pastors. Reply: Alphonsus de Castro more correctly holds, in book 1 against heresies, chapter 6, that all priests are pastors.

units.la: Idem profitetur Salmeron Jesuita comm. in Eph. 4. disp. 10. §. per pastores. Per pastores intelligi episcopos & presbyteros uni civitati pascendae affixos, & curam animarum habentes, quibus est annexum officium docendi, quo oves suas pascat.
units.tr: Salmeron the Jesuit professes the same, in his commentary on Eph. 4, disputation 10, §. "by pastors." By pastors are understood bishops and presbyters attached to one city to be fed, and having the care of souls, to whom is joined the office of teaching, by which they feed their sheep.

units.la: Item in 1. Tim. 4. disp. 13. Mitra, quae capiti episcopi superponitur gemi-nata, duorum testamentorum scientiam, quae tradere debet, denotat.
units.tr: Likewise, on 1 Tim. 4, disputation 13: the mitre placed upon the bishop's head, being doubled, denotes the knowledge of the two Testaments, which he ought to hand on.

units.la: Deinde, quid judicabunt illi, qui non sunt theologi, neque divinarum rerum scientia pollent? tales autem sunt complures in papatu. Audi itaque quid statuat Arelatensis Cardinalis, sicut refert Æneas Sylvius de gestis Concil. Basiliensis. Visum est nobis & Spiritui sancto, inquit Jacobus in concilio Hierosolymitano. Vox (nobis) refertur ad illud, quod praecessit, ubi nominatur apostoli & seniores & verbum (visum est) nō cōsultatione illius sed decisione significat: Quid prohibet exemplū apostolicum imitari? In concilio Niceno primo Athanasius presbyter ferè solus argumentationes Arianorum disturbabat. Constantiē sis synodi recens memoria est, ubi ego, qui nondum Cardinalis vel episcopus, sed tantum doctor eram, interfui, vidiqué sine difficultate inferiores cum episcopis ad decisionem rerum admitti arduarum. Quin etiam in Pisano concilio, & amplissimo Lateranensi judicasse presbyteros una cum episcopis non est ambiguum: præterea, si Abbates, ut in omnibus concilijs observatum vidimus, vocem habent decisivā, qui tamen ordines à Christo instituti non fuerunt, cur non presbyteri: quorum ordinem Christus per discipulos instituit? si soli episcopi, ut Panormitanus vult, vocem decisivam habent; ubi nunc fides catholica, quū præsertim episcopi deliciis indulgeant? {13} Episcopos habere auctoritatem decidendi, non propter præstantiam doctridoctrina, sed propter ecclesiasticam jurisdi-ctionem, quam habent ut persona publica & principes. Respondeat Stella in Luc. 6. in illa verba. Numquid potest cæ-cus cęcum ducere. Qui fieri potest, inquit, ut adversus hæreses disputet, qui non est theologus? quod si responderis, quod hi episcopi secum ducunt doctos theologos, qui eos illuminent & doceant, quid dicturi sint (ut in nostro concilio Tridentino nostris temporibus contigit) in hac quidem re non possum mihi a risu temperare, melius sane episcopi facerent, si episcopatus suos theologis renunciarent, de his vera est Domini sententia, si cæcus cæcū ducit &c. Desinant itaque illi iurati pontificis Romani gloriari atq; imponere populo Christiano solis & inanibus titulis. Audi Paulum ad Tit. 1.8, quod episcopus & pastor sit, qui sit tenax fidelis illius sermonis qui ad doctrinam facit, ut possit & exhortari doctrina sana & contradicentes convincere. His assentitur Toletus Jes. instruct. sacerd. l. 1. cap. ult.§. Episcop°. Episcopus est, inquit, cui dictum est 1.Pet.1. Paratiestote reddere rationem omni poscenti de eâ quæ vobis est, fide. Unde perfecta utriusque testamenti debet habere cognitionem, & perfectam mysteriorum fidei intelligentiam, ut sciat etiam aliis veritatem fidei exponere, & aliorum contra veritatem fallacias exponere, hæresesque expugnare. {34} Pontifici Romano & patribus Tridentinis nihil aliud fuisse propositum, quam ut e medio tollerent schismatum et hæresewn auctores, atque ecclesiæ pacem restituerent. Resp. Resipsa ostendit, utra pars dogmata manifeste falsa & cultus idololatricos tueri ac propagare studeat. Vide catalogu Romanensium traditionum, & similia loca. Utinam videamus aliquando Constantinos, Theodosios, qui ingemiscenti ecclesiæ succurrant! & omnibus apparebit, utra pars lucem fugiat, & legitima judicia reformidet; præcludetur etiam per Dei gratiam occasio majoribus distractionibus animorum, atque opinio-nionionum confusionibus : & con-tra animi vulnerati utrinq; lenien-tur ad Dei gloriam & salutem pu-blicam.
units.tr: Next, what will those judge who are not theologians and do not excel in the knowledge of divine things? Yet such are numerous under the papacy. Hear then what the Cardinal of Arles lays down, as Aeneas Sylvius reports in his account of the Council of Basel. "It seemed good to us and to the Holy Spirit," said James in the council of Jerusalem. The word "us" refers to what went before, where the apostles and elders are named, and the word "it seemed good" signifies not consultation but decision. What prevents us from imitating the apostolic example? In the first Council of Nicaea, the presbyter Athanasius almost alone confounded the arguments of the Arians. The recent memory of the Council of Constance is still fresh, where I, who was not yet a cardinal or bishop but only a teacher, took part, and I saw that inferiors were admitted without difficulty with the bishops to the decision of weighty matters. Moreover, it is not doubtful that in the council of Pisa, and in the very ample Lateran council, presbyters judged together with the bishops. Besides, if abbots, as we have seen observed in all councils, have a decisive vote, though their orders were not instituted by Christ, why not presbyters, whose order Christ instituted through the disciples? If only bishops, as Panormitanus wishes, have a decisive vote, where then is the Catholic faith, especially since bishops indulge in pleasures? {13} Bishops have the authority to decide not because of superiority of teaching, but because of ecclesiastical jurisdiction, which they hold as public persons and princes. Let Stella on Luke 6 answer on those words, "Can the blind lead the blind?" "How can it be," he says, "that one disputes against heresies who is not a theologian?" But if you should answer that these bishops bring along learned theologians with them, who enlighten and teach them, what are they going to say (as happened in our own time at our council of Trent)? In this matter I cannot refrain from laughter. Truly, the bishops would do better to resign their bishoprics to the theologians. Of these the Lord's saying is true: "If the blind lead the blind," etc. Let them therefore cease, those sworn to the Roman pontiff, to boast and to impose on the Christian people with empty titles alone. Hear Paul, Tit. 1.8, that a bishop and pastor is one who holds fast to the faithful word that accords with doctrine, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to convict those who contradict. Toletus the Jesuit agrees with this, in Instruction of Priests, book 1, last chapter, §. Bishop. "A bishop," he says, "is one to whom it is said in 1 Pet. 1: 'Be ready always to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the faith that is in you.'" Hence he must have a perfect knowledge of both Testaments and a perfect understanding of the mysteries of faith, so that he may know how to expound the truth of the faith to others, to expose the fallacies of others against the truth, and to overthrow heresies. {34} The Roman pontiff and the Fathers of Trent proposed nothing else than to remove from the midst the authors of schisms and heresies, and to restore peace to the Church. Reply: The thing itself shows which side manifestly strives to defend and propagate false doctrines and idolatrous worship. See the catalogue of Romanist traditions, and similar passages. Would that we might one day see Constantines and Theodosiuses, who would come to the aid of the groaning Church! Then it will be apparent to all which side shuns the light and dreads lawful judgments. The occasion for greater divisions of minds and confusions of opinions will also be closed off, by the grace of God, and on the contrary the wounded spirits on both sides will be soothed, to the glory of God and the public salvation.

units.la: REFVTATIO ARGVMEN-tationum pontificiarum ad confir-mandum bannum,&anathe-mata sedis Roma-na.
units.tr: A REFUTATION OF THE PAPAL ARGUMENTS FOR CONFIRMING THE BAN AND ANATHEMAS OF THE ROMAN SEE.

units.la: AJunt constare ex Matt. 18.18. ex-communicatione ab ecclesia, vel successoribus Petri et apostolorum pronunciatam esse maximi momenti apud Deum: ejusque horrendum exemplū cerni in Anania et Saphirâ Act. 5.1. Corinthio incestuoso 1.Cor.5.9. pseudapostolis illis Gal.1.8.9. Hymenaeo et Alexandro 1.Tim.1.20. et similibus. Resp. Equidem excommunicatio legitima est magni poderis apud Deum: at excommunicationes atq; anathemata Romanensium sunt illegitima, quod probavimus antea. 2 Omnibus seculis poenam excommunicationis fuisse maximè formidabilem in ecclesia, Resp. Ita, ubi videlicet censores fuerunt Dei instrumenta, atque ex Dei verbo reus legitimo verae ecclesiae judicio fuit damnatus: alioqui praestat ad exemplum confessorum Christi &a[?], postolorum[?] ejici ex consortio impiorum, quàm inter eos numerari.*
units.tr: They say it is established from Matt. 18.18 that excommunication pronounced by the Church, or by the successors of Peter and the apostles, is of the greatest moment before God. Its dreadful example is seen in Ananias and Sapphira, Acts 5.1; in the incestuous Corinthian, 1 Cor. 5.9; in those false apostles, Gal. 1.8-9; in Hymenaeus and Alexander, 1 Tim. 1.20; and in similar cases. Reply: Indeed, lawful excommunication is of great weight before God, but the excommunications and anathemas of the Romanists are unlawful, as we have proved above. 2 In all ages the penalty of excommunication has been most dreaded in the Church. Reply: So it has been, namely where the censors were instruments of God and the accused was condemned by the legitimate judgment of the true Church according to God's word. Otherwise, after the example of the confessors of Christ and of the apostles, it is better to be cast out from the company of the impious than to be numbered among them.

units.la: 3 Hanc esse perpetuam ecclesiae praxin, quod excommunicationis sententia, judicium, potestas fuerint penes praelatos, comprimus vero pontificem Romanum ejusque Cardinales & legatos. Resp. Ab auctoritate veterum episcoporum piorum, & ecclesiae Romanae veteris ad praesules hodiernos Romanos non valet consequentia. Qui enim nunc sunt, defecerunt cum capite suo pontifi-ce à Domino nostro Iesu Christo & veritate euangelica. Deinde neque hoc sequitur: Longo usu praesules Romani hanc potestatem sibi arro-garunt: ergo jure eam tenent. Plura vide in Medulla Papismi in locis de pontifice, & ecclesia Romana. + Instant ex 1.Cor.5.1.à solo Paulo incestuosum esse excommunicatum. Resp. Primùm non sequitur, licere episcopo, quod-cunque fecerunt apostoli. Deinde apostolus praeit quidem Corinthiis suo judicio, attamen neutiquam derogat eis jus ecclesiæ a Christo traditum Matth.18. Dic ecclesiæ. Imò verò etiam judicium eis tribuit, qui ait, An non vos judicatis de iis, qui intus sunt: similiter dicit, tradatur Satanæ vid. à vobis. Idque illorum & suo spiritu in nomine Domini nostri Jesu Christi congregatis. Item v. 7. Expurgate igitur vetus fermentum, scil. vos. & v. 13. Tollite igitur istum improbum ex vobis ipsis. s Apostolum velle Corinthios congregari non ut judices, sed ut exsecutores, neque illos assumere in judicando socios; sed totam judicandi potestatem in uno Paulo ejusque spiritu, in nomine ac virtute Christi residere. Resp. Sicuti auctoritas Christi non tollit judicium apostoli: Itaque auctoritas apostoli tollit judicium ecclesiæ: sed sunt subordinata.
units.tr: 3 That this has been the perpetual practice of the Church: the sentence, the judgment and the power of excommunication have rested with the prelates, while the Roman pontiff and his cardinals and legates are included. Reply: The inference from the authority of the ancient pious bishops and of the old Roman church to the present Roman prelates does not hold. For those who now exist have fallen away, together with their head the pontiff, from our Lord Jesus Christ and from the gospel truth. Nor does this follow: "By long usage the Roman prelates have arrogated this power to themselves; therefore they hold it by right." See more in the Medulla Papismi, under the headings on the pontiff and the Roman church. + They press from 1 Cor. 5.1 that the incestuous man was excommunicated by Paul alone. Reply: First, it does not follow that it is lawful for a bishop to do whatever the apostles did. Second, the apostle indeed goes before the Corinthians with his judgment, yet he by no means derogates from the right of the Church, handed down by Christ in Matt. 18: "Tell it to the Church." Indeed he even grants them judgment, when he says, "Do not you judge those who are within?" Likewise he says, "let him be delivered to Satan," namely by you, and by their spirit and his, gathered in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Likewise in v. 7: "Purge out therefore the old leaven," namely you; and in v. 13: "Put away from among yourselves that wicked person." That the Apostle wills the Corinthians to be gathered not as judges but as executors, nor to take them as partners in judging, but that the whole power of judging resides in Paul alone and his spirit, in the name and power of Christ. Reply: Just as the authority of Christ does not remove the judgment of the apostle, so the authority of the apostle does not remove the judgment of the Church; but they are subordinate.

units.la: Hæc equidem sufficiunt, sed nequid deest numero argumentationem redeunt ad crambem sæpius recoctam, & inculcant ac prædicant prolixè titulos & potestatem pontificiam Romanorum: quod sint præsides & monarmonarcha totius ecclesiæ militantis, & habeant supremam, generalem, et absolutam potestatem mandandi et vetandi. ¶.
units.tr: These indeed suffice; but lest anything be lacking in number of arguments, they return to the crambe reheated too often, and they inculcate and proclaim at length the titles and power of the Roman pontiffs: that they are presidents and monarch of the whole militant Church, and have supreme, general and absolute power of commanding and forbidding. ¶

units.la: Id genus sexcenta proferre poteris. Imò infinita occurrunt in lectione scholasticorum extremæ impietatis pontificiæ testimonia. Glossa in præf. Clement. eum profitetur neque Deum esse, neque hominem sed neutrum inter utrumque Distinct. 96. cap. satis gloriatur autem & gaudet Papa se Deum appellari à Constantino: Ibidem dicitur porrò, eum à seculari potestate neque ligari prorsus neque solvi posse. At Deo gratias habemus, quòd patefactus sit homo ille peccati, filius ille perditionis, sese opponens ille & efferés supra quicquid dicitur Deus, præ se ferés se esse Deum. Revelatus est per Dei gratiam sceleratus ille, quem Dominus absumit spiritu oris sui & illustri adventu suo abolebit. 2. Thess. 2. 3. et seq. Ubique cerni virtutem auctoritatis pontificiæ, si res deveniat ad banni executionem.
units.tr: You may bring forth six hundred such things of this kind. Indeed, in reading the scholastics, countless testimonies of extreme papal impiety occur. The Gloss on the preface to the Clementines professes that he is neither God nor man but something between the two. Distinction 96, chapter Satis, he boasts and rejoices that the Pope was called God by Constantine. Ibidem it is further said that he can be neither bound nor loosed at all by secular power. But thanks be to God, we have that the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who sets himself against and exalts himself above everything called God, displaying himself as God. That wicked one is revealed through the grace of God, whom the Lord will consume with the breath of his mouth and abolish by his glorious coming. 2 Thess. 2.3 and following. Everywhere the power of papal authority is seen, if the matter comes to the execution of the ban.

units.la: Resp. Ita sanè ejus adventus est ex illa vi efficaci satanæ cum omni po-ten. tentia & signis ac prodigiis menda-cibus, & cum omni seductione injustitiæ in iis qui pereunt, quiqué acquieverunt in injustitia 2.thes.2.9. at nos perstabilihus Dei beneficio & retinebimus traditam doctrinam, quam edocti sumus & per sermonem & per epistolam, vid. apostolorum, cæterorumque Spiritus s. amanuensium.
units.tr: Reply: Indeed, his coming is according to the powerful working of Satan, with all power and lying signs and wonders, and with all deceit of unrighteousness among those who perish, because they took pleasure in unrighteousness (2 Thess. 2.9). But we, by the benefit of God, will stand firm and retain the doctrine handed down, which we have been taught both by word and by letter, namely by the apostles and the other amanuenses of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: §[?] Non leve crimen esse, imò detestandum, si quis contemnat vele-[?]tiam negligat ecclesiæ censuram, minas, bannū etc.
units.tr: It is no slight crime, indeed a detestable one, if anyone despises, or even neglects, the censure, threats, ban, etc. of the Church.

units.la: §[?] Quod dictū est sæpius[?], nō est quæstio de cēsurā verę ecclesiæ, sed agitur de banno pōtificis & clerici Romani, ejusque nullitatem argumentis firmis & solidis probavimus. Audi prętęrea declarationem Canonistarū In causa 11.q.3. c.Temerarium. Temerariū judicium plerumq; nihil nocet ei, de quo temere judicatur, ei autem qui temerè judicat, ipsa temeritas necesse est noceat. Item cap. sequ. Quid obest homini, quód ex illa tabula vult illum delere humana ignorantia, si de libro vive-tium non deleat iniqua conscientia.
units.tr: As has often been said, the question is not about the censure of the true Church; the matter at issue is the ban of the pontiff and the Roman clergy, and we have proved its nullity by firm and solid arguments. Hear moreover the declaration of the canonists. In cause 11, q. 3, c. Temerarium: "A rash judgment mostly does no harm to him about whom it is rashly made, but to him who judges rashly the rashness itself necessarily does harm." Likewise the next chapter: "What harm is it to a man that human ignorance wishes to blot him out of that tablet, if an unjust conscience does not blot him out of the book of the living?"

units.la: Et cap. Etsi. Etsi damnatis ab homine, aliud est sella terrena, aliud est tribunal cœleste: ab inferiore accipit sententiam, à superiore coronâ. Notatu etiam dignum est, quod legitur cap. Illud plane. Illud plane non temere dixerim, quod si quisquam fidelium fuerit anathemati satus injustè, potius ei oberit qui facit, quàm qui hanc patitur injuriam. Spiritus enim sanctus habitans in sanctis, per quē quisque ligatur aut solvitur, immeritā nulli ingerit poenam. Quæcunq; ergo in nos vibrat pontifex cū suis juratis anathemata, necessum est ut tandem redundent in capita maledicentium: nos interea studebimus inservire Domino Deo nostro ex praescripto verbi prophetici & apostolici, bona conscientiâ. 9 Deum severiore vindicta ulcisci eos, qui ipsius ordinationi resistunt.
units.tr: And chapter Etsi: "Although one is condemned by man, it is one thing to be an earthly seat, another a heavenly tribunal: from the lower one receives a sentence, from the higher a crown." It is also worth noting what is read in chapter Illud plane: "I would not say this rashly: if any of the faithful has been unjustly struck with anathema, the harm falls rather on him who does it than on him who suffers this injury. For the Holy Spirit, dwelling in the saints, by whom each is bound or loosed, inflicts no undeserved punishment on anyone. Therefore, whatever the pontiff hurls at us with his sworn anathemas must in the end recoil on the heads of those who curse; meanwhile we will study to serve the Lord our God, according to the prescription of the prophetic and apostolic word, with a good conscience." 9 God avenges with a heavier vengeance those who resist his ordinance.

units.la: Resp. Benedicet autem eis, qui exeunt Româ, quiq; aversantur synagogam pontificiam: quia facta est Babylon, sicuti docuimus antea, & officina omnium scelerum & haeresion. scn̄.¹⁰ Protestantit. atq; omnibus hære-ticis esse in more positum, ut calumnientur sedem Romanam. Resp. Dicere quod res est, non est calumniati. Si vis, cō-sule doctores Iesuitas, quos notavi-mus in Medulla Papismi in loco de ecclesia Romana. Audi præterea Mantuanum
units.tr: Reply: Rather, he will bless those who go out of Rome and turn away from the papal synagogue, because it has become Babylon, as we taught before, and the workshop of all crimes and heresies. 10 It is the custom of Protestants and of all heretics to slander the Roman see. Reply: To say what is the case is not to slander. If you wish, consult the Jesuit doctors, whom we noted in the Medulla Papismi under the heading on the Roman church. Hear moreover Mantuan:

units.la: Ipudor in villas, si non patiuntur easdem / Et villæ vomicas: Roma est jam tota lu-panar.
units.tr: Shame upon the villages, if they do not suffer the same sores as the villages: Rome is now wholly a brothel.

units.la: Item
units.tr: Likewise:

units.la: Venalia Romæ: / Tepla, sacerdotes, altaria, sacra, corona, / Ignis, thura, preces, cœlum est venale, / Deusque.
units.tr: Things for sale at Rome: temples, priests, altars, sacred things, the crown, fire, incense, prayers; heaven is for sale, and God too.

units.la: His assentitur Petrarcha in epi-stol. Quicquid de Assyria, vel de Æ-gyptia, Babylone, quicquid de Labyrinthis, quicquid deniq; de Averni limine, deq; tartareis sylvis-sulphu-ribus legitur, huic Tartaro (Romæ) admotum fabula est. Hic turrificus simul & terrificus Nimrod: hic pha-retrata Semiramis, hic inexorabilis Minos, hic Rhadamantus, hic Cerberus universa devorans. Hic tauro supposita Pasiphaë, mixtumq; genus, quod Maro inquit, prolesque biformis, Minotaurus inest, veneris monimenta nefandæ. Hîc postremò quicquid atrum, quicquid horribile usquam est aut fingitur aspicias: & ut breviter dicam, scelerum ac dedecorum sententia, "Pios veteres longè aliter sensisse de Pontifice Romano, ejusq; judiciis Resp. Audi ergo Bernhardum lib. 4. de confid. ad Eugen. Papam cap. 1. Quem dabis mihi de tota maxima urbe, qui te in papam receperit, precio, seu spe precii non interveniente. Hi invisi terra & cœlo, utrique injecere manus: impii in Deum, temerarii in sanctos, seditio-si in invicem. En judicium antiquitatis. Plura notavimus suis locis, & comprimis demonstravimus, quàm graviter à veritate evangelicâ pontifices Romani aberrarint in hunc usque diem. Quâ igitur conscien-tiâ, quaeso, ab illorum auctoritate de-pendebimus? Audiamus ergo Chri-sti Spiritum in Scripturâ loquen-tem: & nihil nobis de-crit.
units.tr: Petrarch agrees with these in his letter: whatever is read of Assyria, or of Egypt and Babylon, whatever of the labyrinths, whatever finally of the threshold of Avernus and the sulphurous Tartarean woods, is a fable compared with this Tartarus (Rome). Here is the tower-building and terror-striking Nimrod; here the Pharaoh-like Semiramis; here the inexorable Minos, here Rhadamanthus, here Cerberus devouring everything. Here is Pasiphaë placed under the bull, and the mixed race which Maro calls the two-formed offspring, the Minotaur, monument of unspeakable lust. Here, finally, whatever is black, whatever is horrible anywhere, is or is imagined, you will see; and to put it briefly, a sentence of crimes and disgraces. That the pious ancients thought quite otherwise about the Roman pontiff and his judgments. Reply: Hear then Bernard, book 4 On Consideration, to Pope Eugene, chapter 1: "Whom will you give me, out of the whole great city, who would receive you as pope without price, or without the hope of price intervening? These men, hated by earth and heaven, have laid hands on both: impious toward God, rash toward the saints, seditious toward one another." See the judgment of antiquity. We have noted more in their proper places, and especially demonstrated how gravely the Roman pontiffs have strayed from evangelical truth down to this day. With what conscience, I ask, shall we depend on their authority? Let us therefore hear the Spirit of Christ speaking in Scripture, and nothing will be lacking to us.

units.la: Merito excommunicari eos, qui citati vocati venire noluerunt ad concilium legitimum. resp. Tridentinum autem non fuisse legitimum docuimus antea. deinde potestantes non potuerunt venire Tridentum, sine evidenti capitis periculo: quia antequam essent auditi, fuerunt damnati; testibus actis concilii, & toto eius processu. Rectius fecisse prote-stantes, si causam suam publicè in pleno con-cilio defendissent. resp. Quod dixi, non licuit: quia non alii fuerunt annumerati patribus, quàm jurati pontificis Romani, neq; libera fuerunt suffragia. Decuisse protestantes, ut etiam cum capitis periculo causam suam de-fendissent. resp. Si ita conduxissent ad Dei gloriam & ecclesiae aedifica-cationem: rectius autem tum principes tum doctores ecclesiarū prospexerunt gregi sibi comisso, quòd substituerunt in suis territoriis, atque argumentis firmis ac solidis demonstrarunt illius concilii Tridentini nullitatem. Decere omnes & singu-
units.tr: Those who, when cited and summoned, refused to come to a lawful council are rightly excommunicated. Reply: We have shown above that the Council of Trent was not lawful. Moreover, the Protestants could not come to Trent without evident danger to their heads, since they were condemned before they were heard, as the acts of the council and its whole proceedings bear witness. The Protestants would have acted more rightly had they defended their cause publicly in the full council. Reply: I have said that this was not permitted, since none were counted among the Fathers except those sworn to the Roman pontiff, and the votes were not free. The Protestants ought to have defended their cause even at the risk of their heads. Reply: They would have done so if they had thought it would lead to God's glory and the building up of the Church. But the princes and the teachers of the churches rightly looked after the flock committed to them when they set up their own territories, and they demonstrated by firm and solid arguments the nullity of that Council of Tent... It becomes all and each of the faithful

units.la: [Marginal strip of facing page: illegible, ~60 letters] los[?] fideles, ut citati & rogati reddant ra-tionem suæ professionis & fidei. Christus autem etiam conticuisse legitur ad interrogata pharisæorum & sacerdotum. 16 Complures ex episcopis Romanis satis multa castigasse & damnasse, quæ longo usu obtinuerant in curia pontificis & ecclesiâ: felicius ergo plura corrigi potuisse, si doctores protestantium sese illis adjunxissent. resp. Protestantium doctores non sunt accersiti, ut cum aliis disceptarent & judicarent controversias religionis, sed ut audirent sententiam, videlicet damnatoriam, si decretis pontificis & cleri Romani parere nol-lent: sicuti docuimus supra pa. 76.
units.tr: [Marginal strip of facing page: illegible, ~60 letters] all and each of the faithful, to be cited and asked, to give an account of their profession and faith. Yet it is read that Christ also kept silent when questioned by the Pharisees and the priests. 16 Several of the Roman bishops have rebuked and condemned quite a lot of what had been retained by long custom in the papal court and the Church; so more could have been corrected more happily, if the teachers of the Protestants had joined themselves to them. Reply: The teachers of the Protestants were not summoned so that they might dispute and judge controversies of religion with the others, but so that they might hear a sentence, namely a condemnatory one, if they were unwilling to obey the decrees of the Roman pontiff and clergy; as we have shown above, p. 76.

units.la: Deinde licet quidam ex doctoribus pontificiis liberius locuti sint, & castigaverint impietatem cleri, tamen omnes & singuli subjecerunt se placitis pontificis, tanquam supremi judicis: omnes namque fuerunt Romanæ sedi obstricti juramento, cujus summam notavimus supra p. 75.
units.tr: Furthermore, although some of the Papist teachers have spoken more freely and have rebuked the impiety of the clergy, nevertheless all and each of them submitted themselves to the decisions of the pontiff as supreme judge; for all of them were bound to the Roman See by oath, the substance of which we noted above, p. 75.

units.la: QVA RATIONE VIRI PII certi esse possint de veritate professionis suæ?
units.tr: BY WHAT REASON PIOUS MEN CAN BE CERTAIN OF THE TRUTH OF THEIR PROFESSION

units.la: Quæritur, Quæ sit tutissima via et ratio confirmandi animos piorum de veritate professionis suæ. ℞. Ad hoc idem responderi posset, quod dictum est suis locis, de mediis inquirendi genuinum scripturæ sensum, & decidendi controversias.
units.tr: The question is: What is the safest way and method of confirming the minds of the pious concerning the truth of their profession? Answer: The same answer could be given to this as has been given in their places, concerning the means of inquiring into the genuine sense of Scripture and of deciding controversies.

units.la: Verum, ut paulo felicius, quæ nobis præfiximus, scopū asequamur, summam eorum, quæ aliàs prolixè de hoc argumento disseruntur, complectemur, & dicimus: Si quis velit confirmari de professionis suæ veritate, & legitimè dijudicare controversias.
units.tr: But, so that we may reach our aim a little more happily, we will embrace the sum of those things which are elsewhere discussed at length on this subject, and we say: If anyone wishes to be confirmed in the truth of his profession, and to judge controversies lawfully:

units.la: 1 Faciat initium à precibus ad Deum.
units.tr: (1) Let him begin with prayer to God.

units.la: 2 Valere jussis[?] præjudiciis hoc unicum sibi proponat, ut erudiatur & confirmetur de dogmatum veritate ad Dei gloriam, suam salutem, aliorumq; exædificationem.
units.tr: (2) Having put aside prejudices, let him set before himself this one aim: that he may be taught and confirmed in the truth of the doctrines, to the glory of God, his own salvation, and the edification of others.

units.la: 3 Eligat catechesin vel auctorem, quem vel didicerit in tenerâ ætate, vel quemcunque voluerit.
units.tr: (3) Let him choose a catechism or an author, either one he learned in tender age or whichever he likes.

units.la: 4 Examinet singula doctrinæ loca distinctè, piè, & accuratè: tum quæ fidem, tum quæ mores spectant.
units.tr: (4) Let him examine the individual places of doctrine distinctly, piously and accurately, both those which concern faith and those which concern morals.

units.la: 5 Instituat iustam anatomen singulorum articulorum, capitum, periodorum.
units.tr: (5) Let him make a proper analysis of the individual articles, chapters and periods.

units.la: 6 Opponat deinde confessionem adversantium vel dissentientium.
units.tr: (6) Then let him set against them the confession of their opponents or dissenters.

units.la: 7 Inquirat, in quibus ergo doctores dissentiant, & quis sit verus & genuinus controversiarum status.
units.tr: (7) Let him inquire in what points the teachers disagree, and what is the true and genuine state of the controversies.

units.la: 8 Singula capita accuratè & distinctè comprehendat, & notet verbis propriis & perspicuis, breviter & nudè, omisso rhetorum ornatu.
units.tr: (8) Let him grasp each head accurately and distinctly, and note it in proper and perspicuous words, briefly and plainly, omitting the ornament of the rhetoricians.

units.la: 9 Distinguat creditu necessaria, à minus necessariis.
units.tr: (9) Let him distinguish what is necessary to believe from what is less necessary.

units.la: 10 Distinguat etiam quæstiones proprie & verè theologicas à scholasticis & philosophicis.
units.tr: (10) Let him also distinguish questions that are properly and truly theological from scholastic and philosophical ones.

units.la: 11 Accuratè item notet quæstiones curiosas, frivolas: vel de quibus dissentire licet, salvo fraternitatis & charitatis Christianæ vinculo.
units.tr: (11) Let him likewise accurately note curious and frivolous questions, or those on which it is permitted to differ without loss of the bond of Christian brotherhood and charity.

units.la: 12 Observet non minus de quibus tacere satius sit in ecclesia & apud populum Dei: quia etiam aliqua e-rudita inscitia est.
units.tr: (12) Let him observe, no less, what it is better to keep silent about in the Church and among the people of God, since some ignorance is also a kind of learning.

units.la: 13 Perpendat praeterea, quibus argumentis utraque pars sua exponat & confirmet.
units.tr: (13) Let him further weigh with what arguments each side sets out and confirms its position.

units.la: 14 Attendat quid iisdem verbis, quibus proponitur in scriptura, expressum sit, quibus anima pia simpliciter, tuto, & necessario acquie-scit.
units.tr: (14) Let him attend to what is expressed in the very words in which it is set forth in Scripture, which a pious soul rests in simply, safely and necessarily.

units.la: 15 Deinde quid exprimatur in scripturis verbis synonymis vel idem significantibus.
units.tr: (15) Then, what is expressed in Scripture by synonymous words or words having the same meaning.

units.la: 16 Similiter etiam, quid ex conse-quenti inde eruatur & cõcludatur.
units.tr: (16) Likewise, what is drawn out and concluded from it by consequence.

units.la: 17 Et contra disspiciat; Quodnam dogma pugnet cum expressis s. scri-pturae testimoniis: aut eorum consequentibus.
units.tr: (17) And, on the contrary, let him see what doctrine conflicts with the express testimonies of Holy Scripture, or with their consequences.

units.la: 18 Atque ita controversa diiudicet ad earundem s. scripturarum amussim & regulam.
units.tr: (18) And thus let him decide the controversies by the plumb-line and rule of the same Holy Scriptures.

units.la: 19 Ad calumnias autem, probra, invectivas aures atque oculos obsir-met.
units.tr: (19) As for calumnies, reproaches and invectives, let him close his ears and eyes.

units.la: 20 Postremum potestā doctiorib. vel magis exercitatis inquiri cōsensus antiquitatis, atque aliorum doctorum orthodoxorum.
units.tr: (20) Lastly, let him, if he is more learned or more practised, inquire into the consent of antiquity and of other orthodox teachers.

units.la: DE AUCTORITATE MAGISTRATUS in dijudicandis fidei controversiis.
units.tr: ON THE AUTHORITY OF THE MAGISTRATE IN JUDGING CONTROVERSIES OF FAITH

units.la: Quaeritur, An principibus, et aliis politicis viris concedi debeat judicium de rebus fidei? &. Romani pontificii negant. Orthodoxi protestātes affirmant.
units.tr: The question is: Ought judgment on matters of faith to be granted to princes and other civil men? The Roman Papists deny it; the orthodox Protestants affirm it.

units.la: Orthodoxa sententia probatur. Quia Deuter. 17. 18. 19. jubetur regibus, ut describant sibi exemplum legis in libro, ex eo qui in cōspectu sacerdotum Leviticorum. Item ut sit penes regem, & legat in eo omnib. diebus vitae suae; ut discat timere Jehovam Deum suum. Hinc liquet, magistratui singulariter & divinitus esse mandatum, ut sit custos utriusq; tabulae.
units.tr: The orthodox view is proved. Because in Deut. 17.18, 19 kings are commanded to write out for themselves a copy of the law in a book, from that which is before the Levitical priests; and likewise that it should be with the king, and that he should read in it all the days of his life, so that he may learn to fear Jehovah his God. From this it is clear that it was singularly and divinely commanded to the magistrate that he should be the guardian of both tables.

units.la: Ideo 1. Reg. 11. 21. regi Joas cum inauguraretur datus est in manus liber legis Dei. Propterea etiam Rom. 13. 1. 4. 6, magistratus vocatur [illegible, ~6 letters]ὁ & λειτουργὸς[?] Dei. Similiter Exod. 22.28. & Psal.82.5.6. dicuntur Elo-him (Dii) & filii excelsi: quia sunt vicarii Dei. Item Psal.48.7v. Esa.49v. 23. nutritii ecclesiæ Christi, & Ezec. 34.23. vocantur patres.
units.tr: Therefore, in 2 Kings 11.12 (1 Kings 11.21 in the text as printed), when Joash was inaugurated, the book of God's law was put into his hands. For this reason also, in Rom. 13.1, 4, 6, the magistrate is called a minister [διάκονος] and servant [λειτουργὸς] of God. Similarly, in Exod. 22.28 and Ps. 82.5, 6 they are called Elohim (gods) and sons of the Most High, because they are vicars of God. Likewise, in Ps. 48.7 and Isa. 49.23 they are the nursing fathers of Christ's Church, and in Ezek. 34.23 they are called fathers.

units.la: Idem confirmat exempla sancto-rum veterum, Mosis, Davidis 1.Chr. 13.5. & 22. & seq. Solomonis 2.Chron. 2. & seq. Ezechiæ 2.Chron.29.5. Josiæ 2.Chron.34.33. & aliorum: qui omnia studio instituerunt ex Dei verbo pu-rum Dei cultum, & è medio sustule-runt quicquid veræ religioni obsta-culo[?]s es[?]se videretur, omnibusq; mo-dis, consiliis & facultatibus eccles-iam, & verbi divini ministerium pro-moverunt: eoque nomine compri-mis laudantur in scriptura. Contra-vero Jud. 21.25. inter vitia anarchias ponitur, quòd non esset rex in Isra-el, & quisq; faceret, quod placebat.
units.tr: The examples of the holy men of old confirm the same: Moses, David (1 Chr. 13.5 and following, and 22 and following), Solomon (2 Chr. 2 and following), Hezekiah (2 Chr. 29.5), Josiah (2 Chr. 34.33) and others, who with zeal set in order, from the Word of God, the pure worship of God, and removed from the midst whatever seemed to be an obstacle to true religion, and by every means, by counsels and by their resources, promoted the Church and the ministry of the divine Word; and for this reason they are especially praised in Scripture. On the contrary, in Judg. 21.25 anarchy is set down among the vices, because there was no king in Israel and everyone did what seemed right to him.

units.la: Huc etiam referri debent præcep-ta illa generalia, quæ ad totam ec-clesiam & singula ejus membra per-tinent. Matth.7.15. Cavete à pseu-doprophetis. Joh.3.39. & 7.17. vult
units.tr: To this should also be referred those general precepts which pertain to the whole Church and to each of its members. Matt. 7.15: Beware of false prophets. John 3.39 (5.39) and 7.17: Christ wills that all should search the Scriptures and know concerning the doctrine whether it is from God.

units.la: Christus, ut omnes scrutentur scri-pturas, & cognoscant de doctrinâ, utrùm ex Deo sit. 1 Thessal. 5. 21. & 1. Joh.4. 1. omnes jubentur scripturas explorare, sibíque à falsa doctrina cavere.
units.tr: 1 Thess. 5.21 and 1 John 4.1: all are commanded to test the Scriptures and to beware of false doctrine.

units.la: Itaque quum omnium prima cura esse debet, scrutari scripturas & probare spiritus, an ex Deo sint ; æquum est ut principes populi singulariter id curent, atque ita omnem operam impendant asserendo honori ejus, cujus sunt vicarii, & cujus beneficio imperant.
units.tr: Therefore, since the first care of all ought to be to search the Scriptures and to test the spirits, whether they are from God, it is right that the princes of the people should take special charge of this, and so bestow all their effort on asserting the honour of him whose vicars they are, and by whose benefit they rule.

units.la: Deinde liquidò ex prædictis apparet, & necessariò colligitur, regum & principum munus esse, Dei cultū juxta scripturam &[?] integrum custodire, & quum collapsus est, ad normam scripturæ instaurare.
units.tr: Furthermore, it clearly appears from what has been said, and is necessarily gathered, that it is the duty of kings and princes to keep the worship of God whole, according to Scripture, and, when it has fallen, to restore it to the norm of Scripture.

units.la: Propterea etiam Act. 25. 11. Apostolus non veretur Cæsarem ejusq; tribunal appellare, quū videret Festum velle gratiam inire à judæis. Et cap. 24. et 26. fidei suæ rationem reddidit coram Felice, & Festo, & Agrippa rege.
units.tr: Therefore also in Acts 25.11 the Apostle does not hesitate to appeal to Caesar and his tribunal, when he saw that Festus wished to win favour with the Jews. And in chapters 24 and 26 he gave an account of his faith before Felix, Festus and King Agrippa.

units.la: Idem probatur, si officium magi-stratus rité attendas. Philosophus lib.5.Ethic.cap.6. magistratum vel principem dicit esse custodem ejus, quod justum est, atqui ita etiam illius quod æquale est, at rectius apostolus Rom. 13. 4. magistratum dicit esse minis-trum Dei, nobis ad bonum, vindicem ad defendenda recte facta, & punien-da delicta gladio.
units.tr: The same is proved if you rightly consider the office of the magistrate. The Philosopher, in Ethics 5, ch. 6, says that the magistrate or prince is the guardian of what is just, and therefore also of what is equal; but more rightly the Apostle, in Rom. 13.4, says that the magistrate is a minister of God for our good, an avenger with the sword to defend right deeds and to punish wrongdoing.

units.la: Hoc si fieri debeat, necesse est, ut primo omnium de constituendo vero Dei cultu cogitet, verā, & maximè incorruptam religionem amplectatur, & sartam tectam, quantum potest, promoveat, atque exemplo pio suis subditis præeat.
units.tr: If this is to be done, he must first of all consider how to establish the true worship of God, embrace the true and especially the purest religion, and advance it, as far as he can, whole and undamaged, going before his subjects with a pious example.

units.la: Atque hæc sunt adeo manifesta, ut neque ex profanis scriptoribus quisquam disseruerit de magistra-tuum officio, ferendis legib. & statu publico, quin à religione & divino cultu fecerit initium.
units.tr: These things are so plain that no profane writer has discussed the duty of magistrates, the enactment of laws and the public order without beginning from religion and divine worship.

units.la: Quomodo autem poterit cogi-tare de constituendo vero Dei cultu, & curare ut verbum Dei incorru-ptè prædicetur, utque omnia recte & legitimè in ecclesia fiant, nisi ju-dicet quid Deus in suo verbo docu-erit, illudq; à fermento & traditio-nibus humanis discernat.
units.tr: But how can he consider how to establish the true worship of God, and take care that the Word of God is preached purely and that everything in the Church is done rightly and lawfully, unless he judges what God has taught in his Word and distinguishes it from leaven and human traditions?

units.la: Jus itaque & potestas judicandi de doctrinâ & capitibus fidei viris principibus adimi nec potest nec debet.
units.tr: Therefore the right and power of judging concerning doctrine and the articles of faith can be taken from princes neither in fact nor in right.

units.la: Idem sentiunt patres orthodoxi, Au-gustinus lib.3.contr.Crescent.cap.51. In hoc reges, sicut divinitus praecipiun-tur, Deo serviunt, si in suo regno bo-na jubeant, mala prohibeant, non solum quae pertinent ad humanam societatem, verum etiam quae ad di-vinam religionem. Socrates lib.5. in proœmio. Ex illo, inquit, tempore, quo imperatores coeperunt esse Christiani, ecclesiae negocia ex eorum nu-tu pendere visa sunt: atq; adeo ma-xima concilia de eorundem senten-tiâ & convocata fuerunt, & adhuc convocantur. Theodoretus lib.1.cap.13. hæc scribit de Constantino Magno. Hic patienter omnia & quietâ intentio-ne ea, quae proponebantur, assume-bat, & vicissim utriusq; partis dicta sustentans paulatim conjungebat secum contetiosos adversarios, nec non placide singulos compellavit oratione Graeca; alios oratione co-ciliabat sibi, alios deterrebat, col-laudatis auctoribus utilis sententiae. Non destitit illos ad concordia ur-gere, donec universos a disceptatio-nibus, in eiusdem sententiae ac do-gmatis unitatem abduceret. Apud Eusebium lib. 4. cap. 37 porro haec habentur de Constantino. Quae ab episcopis in publicis conventibus editae erant regulae, sua consignabat & confirmabat auctoritate, ne reliquarum gentium principibus liceret, quae ab eis decreta essent, abrogare. Plura vide supr. quaest. de concilio Tridentino, pag. 82. 84. et in Medulla papistica pag. 231.
units.tr: The orthodox Fathers likewise hold this view. Augustine, Against Crescentius, book 3, chapter 51: In this respect kings serve God, as they are commanded by God, if in their kingdom they command good things and forbid evil, not only those things which pertain to human society but also those which pertain to the divine religion. Socrates, book 5, in the preface: From the time when the emperors began to be Christians, he says, the affairs of the Church were seen to depend on their nod; and indeed the greatest councils were convened by their judgment, and are convened still. Theodoret, book 1, chapter 13, writes this of Constantine the Great: He patiently and with a calm attention took up all the things that were put forward, and, sustaining the statements of each side in turn, he gradually drew the quarrelsome adversaries to himself; and he addressed each of them mildly in Greek, winning some by his speech, dissuading others, and praising the authors of the sound opinion. He did not cease urging them to concord until he led them all away from the disputes to unity of the same opinion and doctrine. Also in Eusebius, book 4, chapter 37, the following is found about Constantine: The rules which had been issued by the bishops in public assemblies he sealed and confirmed with his own authority, so that it would not be lawful for the princes of the other nations to repeal what had been decreed by them. See more above in the question on the Council of Trent, pp. 82, 84, and in the Medulla papistica, p. 231.

units.la: Testimonia pontificiorum pete ex dicta quaestione de auctoritate concilii Tridentini pag. 86. & seq.
units.tr: For the testimonies of the Papists, seek them in the said question on the authority of the Council of Trent, p. 86 and following.

units.la: Refutatio argumentationum pontificiarum.
units.tr: Refutation of the Papists' arguments.

units.la: Romanenses obiiciunt: Auctori-tatem regalem tantum controversiis carnalibus præsidere. Idq; liquere ex Gen.1. ubi luna præficitur nocti. Lunæ autem meritò comparari præsules politicos, {¶} Pudet sure consultum sine lege loqui: multo magis pudeat theologū sine scriptura pronunciare de fidei controversiis. Deinde ex ipsorum pontificiorum confesso, allegoricum non est argumentativum. {2} 1.Cor.2.15. Tantum spiritualibus tribui judicium omnium. {¶} Spirituales illic dicuntur non tantum clerici vel viri ecclesiastici, pastores, doctores; multo minus præsules Romani: sed omnes regenerati per Christi spiritum. Idque concedit Acosta lib.3. de Christo revelato. {3} Jerem. 21,12. et 22,3. regibus vel principibus hoc tantum denunciari, ut faciant judicium et justitiam, liberent vi oppressum de manu calumniatoris, peregrinum et viduam et pupillum ne contristent, ne injuriam faciant, et sanguinem innocentem ne effundant. Similia legi psal.82,2,3,4. Item Deut.1.16.19. et 17.16. ut audiant causam fratrum suorum, et judicent inter virum et fratrem ejus etc. ne multiplicent sibi equos, neque ad avaritiam ritiam adjiciant animum &c. Hæc autem omnia pertinere ad promotionem posterioris tabulæ: atque ita hoc tantum pertinere ad officium principum, ut sint innocentiæ, modestiæ, honestatis & pacis publicæ protectores ac vindices. ¶. Hæc & similia pertinent ad secundam tabulam. at insulsum est, si quis inde colligat, principes viros tantum juri inter homines dicendo intentos esse debere, neglecta Dei & religionis curâ.† 1. Cor. 6. 4. & seq. juberi, ut fideles controversias suas (politicas) absque civili magistratu privatim dijudicent: ergo multo minus decere pios, ut dependeant à judicio principum in religionis & fidei negocio. ¶. Nihil detrahit apostolus civili jurisdictioni, sed tantum habet rationem sui temporis, quo fieri non potuit, ut coram infidelibus judicibus contenderent fideles, quin variis calumniis essent obnoxii. Itaque monentur Corinthii, tanquam homines litium studiosi, & falsò veram religionem jactantes, ut istiusmodi controversiæ vel semel potius tollantur, vel domestica disceptatione tione componantur.' 1 Cor. 14.29. et 32. prophetarum spiritus tantum prophetis subjici: neque per prophetas intelligi omnes in universum Christianos, sed tantum illos, qui ex legitima vocatione ecclesiam docent. Idq; liquere ex 1 Cor. 12.29. Num omnes prophetae? &. Atqui antea edocti sumus ex Joh. 5. 39. 1 Thess. 5. 21. & 1. Joh. 4. 1. omnibus & singulis fidelibus competere judicium de prophetis & rebus fidei. itaque sciendum est, judicium de rebus fidei (subordinatum videlicet: nam supremum est solius Spiritus S.) esse privatum aut publicum. Privatum competit omnibus & singulis credentibus: testibus praedictis scripturae S. locis, quibus addeillud Christi Johan. 10. 3. & seq. oves vocem ejus (Christi pastoris ovium) audiunt. Item oves eum sequuntur: quia norunt vocem ejus; alienum autem nequaquam sequentur, sed fugient ab eo: quia non norunt vocem alienorum. Publicum competit personis publicis, hoc est ad publicum ecclesiae munus vocatis, quique non tantùm[?] potentiam judicandi habent, sed præterea etiam jus & potestatē suffragandi & judicandi ex legitimâ vocatione. atque hoc intelligit apostolus in loco ad Corinthios, & sensus est, quòd in dijudicādis fidei controversiis præcipuas partes habeant prophetæ atque ecclesiarum doctores.
units.tr: The Papists object: royal authority presides only over carnal controversies. This is clear from Gen. 1, where the moon is set over the night; and it is rightly compared that political leaders are like the moon. It is shameful for a lawyer to speak without the law; much more shameful for a theologian to pronounce on controversies of faith without Scripture. Further, by the Papists' own admission, an allegory is not an argument. (2) 1 Cor. 2:15: Judgment of all things is given only to the spiritual. Here "spiritual" does not mean only clergy or ecclesiastical men, ministers and teachers, much less the Roman prelates, but all who are regenerated by the Spirit of Christ. Acosta concedes this too, in book 3 of De Christo revelato. (3) Jer. 21:12 and 22:3: to kings or princes only this is declared, that they should do judgment and justice, deliver the oppressed out of the hand of the oppressor, not vex the stranger, the widow and the fatherless, do no wrong and shed no innocent blood. Similar things are read in Ps. 82:2–4. Likewise Deut. 1:16, 19 and 17:16: that they should hear the cause of their brethren and judge between a man and his brother, etc., that they should not multiply horses to themselves, nor set their mind on avarice, etc. All these things pertain to the promotion of the second table; and so this alone pertains to the office of princes, that they be guardians and avengers of innocence, modesty, honesty and public peace. These and similar passages pertain to the second table. But it is foolish if someone infers from them that princes ought to be occupied only with dispensing justice among men, neglecting the care of God and religion. 1 Cor. 6:4 and following: the faithful are bidden to settle their (civil) controversies privately without the civil magistrate; therefore much less is it fitting for the godly to depend on the judgment of princes in a matter of religion and faith. The apostle takes nothing from civil jurisdiction, but only has regard to his own time, when it was not possible for the faithful to contend before unbelieving judges without being exposed to various slanders. So the Corinthians are admonished, as men fond of lawsuits and falsely boasting of the true religion, that such controversies should either be removed altogether or rather settled by private arbitration. 1 Cor. 14:29 and 32: the spirits of the prophets are subject only to the prophets; and by "prophets" is understood not all Christians in general, but only those who teach the Church by lawful calling. This is clear from 1 Cor. 12:29: Are all prophets? But we were previously taught from John 5:39, 1 Thess. 5:21 and 1 John 4:1 that the judgment concerning prophets and matters of faith belongs to all and each of the faithful. So it must be understood that judgment concerning matters of faith (subordinate, of course, for the supreme judgment belongs to the Holy Spirit alone) is either private or public. The private kind belongs to all and each of the believers, as the aforesaid passages of Holy Scripture show, to which is added Christ's saying in John 10:3 and following: the sheep hear his voice (the voice of Christ the shepherd of the sheep), and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice; but they will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers. The public kind belongs to public persons, that is, to those called to the public office of the Church, who have not only the power of judging but also the right and power of voting and judging by lawful calling. And this is what the apostle means in the passage to the Corinthians, and the sense is that the prophets and the teachers of the churches have the chief part in deciding controversies of faith.

units.la: 6. Præterea ajunt. Viros politicos non esse satis idoneos ad explicandum difficultates, quæ in s.[?] scripturâ occurrunt. In multis enim scripturâ esse obscuram. Sufficere etiam politicis, ut obediant institutionibus antistitum suorum. ✱. Etiam chri-stiani & pii politici judicare de reli-gione queunt. Imò verò reperiùntur multi plebei, qui cognitione rerum theologicarum multos ex ecclesia-sticis antecunt. Deinde quæ ad salu-tem sunt scitu necessaria perspicuè satis in scripturâ s. proponuntur. Denique non credent pii cuivis spi-ritui, sed probabunt spiritus, an ex Deo sint, vide plura in Medullâ pa-pismi, in loco de verbo Dei. 7. Solùs episcopus competere potestatem judicandi
units.tr: 6. Moreover they say: Political men are not competent enough to explain the difficulties that occur in Holy Scripture. For Scripture is obscure in many places. And it is enough for politicians to obey the directions of their prelates. Even Christian and pious politicians can judge about religion. Indeed many common people are found who surpass many of the ecclesiastics in their knowledge of theological matters. Further, what is necessary to know for salvation is set out clearly enough in Holy Scripture. Finally, the godly do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God; see more in the Medulla papismi, under the heading of the Word of God. 7. The bishop alone has the power of judging.

units.la: Resp. Re-sponsum est antea in loco de concilio Tridentino ad object. 31. 32. & seq. 8 Magistratus debere juri inter homines dicundo intentos esse. Resp. Non tantum, neglecta Dei cura, sed prima eorum cura debet esse, verè religionis & pietatis conservatio: sicuti scripturæ testimoniis & exemplis antea probavimus. 9 Impium esse exponere decisionem controversiarum et regimen ecclesiæ Christi libidini politicorum. Resp. Non dicimus, fas esse, magistratus ut leges de religione contra aut præter Dei verbum suo arbitrio ferat, sed, quod curare debeat, ut Dei cultus, ita ut est ab ipso in verbo præscriptus, purè à ministris evangelii proponatur, & à subditis intelligatur atque observetur, & mota de doctrina fidei controversia ex s. literis decidatur; blasphemi verò & contumaces ecclesiæ turbatores ab urbe Dei arceantur. 10 At viros principes non semper esse pios, neque semper petere regulam imperandi ex lege Dei. Resp. Quòd si impia præcipiat, & scripturæ s. repugnantia, nō est audiendus magistratus politicus; imò verò etiā viros principes monere, castigare & corrigere decet, ad imitationem prophetarum & aliorum fidorum dei servorum. nam semper oportet Deo magis obedire, quàm hominibus.
units.tr: Reply: This has been answered earlier, under the heading of the Council of Trent, at objections 31, 32 and following. 8. Magistrates ought to be intent on dispensing justice among men. Reply: Not only is this not to neglect the care of God, but their first care ought to be the true preservation of religion and piety, as we have already proved by the testimonies and examples of Scripture. 9. It is impious to expose the decision of controversies and the government of Christ's Church to the caprice of politicians.
